  <div class="aip-hero-banner">
    <div class="aip-hero-title">
      API Improvement Proposals
    </div>
    <div class="aip-hero-subtitle">
      Focused design documents for flexible API development.
    </div>
    <div class="aip-buttons">
      <a href="/general" class="glue-button glue-button--high-emphasis">
        Explore the AIPs
      </a>
      <a href="/1" class="glue-button glue-button--high-emphasis">
        Learn how it works
      </a>
      
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="aip-landing-content">
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
    <p>
      AIPs are design documents that summarize Google's API design
      decisions. They also provide a framework and system for others to
      document their own API design rules and practices.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="aip-shortcuts glue-grid glue-grid__col--align-middle">
    
    <div class="aip-shortcut glue-grid__col glue-grid__col--span-6">
      <h1>Curious about the basics?</h1>
      <div>AIPs are a combination of design guidance and a system we use to manage
and track that guidance. Learn more about how the AIP program works in
the first AIP!
</div>
      <a href="/1" class="glue-button glue-button--medium-emphasis">
        Read AIP-1 &raquo;
      </a>
    </div>
    
    <div class="aip-shortcut glue-grid__col glue-grid__col--span-6">
      <h1>Want to help?</h1>
      <div>Interested in helping with AIPs? Contribute by proposing new guidance,
commenting on existing AIPs, or fixing typos. All contributions are
welcome!
</div>
      <a href="/contributing" class="glue-button glue-button--medium-emphasis">
        Contribute to the project &raquo;
      </a>
    </div>
    
    <div class="aip-shortcut glue-grid__col glue-grid__col--span-6">
      <h1>Want to use AIPs for your organization?</h1>
      <div>AIPs are designed to be useful outside of Google. Take a look at how you
might choose which AIPs are best suited to your API design needs.
</div>
      <a href="/adopting" class="glue-button glue-button--medium-emphasis">
        Learn more &raquo;
      </a>
    </div>
    
    <div class="aip-shortcut glue-grid__col glue-grid__col--span-6">
      <h1>Still have questions?</h1>
      <div>Free free to take a look at the <a href="/faq">frequently asked
questions</a>. If you don't find an answer there, file an issue on our
GitHub repository.
</div>
      <a href="https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/issues" class="glue-button glue-button--medium-emphasis">
        Ask us on GitHub &raquo;
      </a>
    </div>

  <h1 id="news">News</h1>
<p>Want to keep up with the AIP system, and what we are working on? Welcome to the
<strong>AIP newsletter</strong>, a monthly publication covering new AIP guidance, and any
other developments useful to API producers.</p>
<h3 id="march-2021">March 2021</h3>
<h5 id="auth-and-field-masks"><a href="/news/2021-03"><strong>Auth and Field Masks</strong></a></h5>
<p>Publishing long-standing guidance around permissions and field masks.</p>
<div class="aip-newsletter-highlights">
  <p>Highlights:</p>
  <ul class="highlights-list">

    <li class="highlight-item">Reviewing:
      <ul>

        <li><a href="/149">AIP-149</a></li>

        <li><a href="/161">AIP-161</a></li>

        <li><a href="/211">AIP-211</a></li>

      </ul>
    </li>


    <li>Approval of AIPs discussed in the October 2020 newsletter.</li>

  </ul>
</div>

<h3 id="october-2020">October 2020</h3>
<h5 id="declarative-friendly-apis"><a href="/news/2020-10"><strong>Declarative-friendly APIs</strong></a></h5>
<p>Why and how to make an API interface "declarative friendly", in order to
enable automation on top of it.</p>
<div class="aip-newsletter-highlights">
  <p>Highlights:</p>
  <ul class="highlights-list">

    <li class="highlight-item">Reviewing:

  </ul>
</div>

<h3 id="april-2020">April 2020</h3>
<h5 id="data-series"><a href="/news/2020-04"><strong>Data Series</strong></a></h5>
<p>This month's AIPs revolve around handling lists and series of data, which
present specific challenges in APIs.</p>

  <h1 id="frequently-asked-questions">Frequently asked questions</h1>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Have a question not answered here? <a href="https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/issues/new?labels=question">Ask us on GitHub!</a></p>
<h3 id="why-protocol-buffers">Why Protocol Buffers?</h3>
<p>At Google, we define all of our APIs using Protocol Buffers (<code>.proto</code> files).
While we realize there are lots of other, newer ways of defining these
interfaces (e.g., OpenAPI, RAML, etc), we had to standardize on something and
since we're Google, we use protos.</p>
<p>This also leads to some very Google-specific ways of mapping proto RPCs to
RESTful URIs (<code>google.api.http</code> annotations). If you're not using protos, feel
free to follow the <em>spirit</em> of the API guidance since you won't be able to
follow the example snippets exactly as provided.</p>
<h3 id="whats-all-this-googley-stuff">What's all this Googley stuff?</h3>
<p>Originally, our API guidance was written by and for Googlers only. We're in the
process of making this guidance more general to the world, but that's far from
complete. If you see things like "Submit a CL" or "Talk to your PA lead", feel
free to send pull requests to fix these oversights.</p>
<p>(CL stands for "Change List" which is sort of like a GitHub Pull Request, and
PA stands for "Product Area" meaning things like "Google Maps" or
"Google Workspace".)</p>
<h3 id="i-like-most-of-these-aips-but-some-make-no-sense-for-me-what-do-i-do">I like most of these AIPs, but some make no sense for me. What do I do?</h3>
<p>Sometimes guidance from AIPs makes lots of sense for Google (perhaps due to its
size or scale) but no sense at all for others. This is much more common than we
originally thought, so we added a way for sub-teams to override guidance that
doesn't make sense for those teams.</p>
<p>If you want to adopt most of the AIPs but have a few that make no sense for
your team, you can override those few and stick to just the ones that make
sense for you.</p>
<h3 id="why-arent-all-of-googles-products-listed-here">Why aren't all of Google's products listed here?</h3>
<p>When this project was first published, the AIP program was still relatively new.
Even with time, not all of Google has adopted AIPs as the way of documenting
their API guidance and policies. We're working on broadening the scope to more
and more areas, both inside and outside Google, so this will continue to evolve.</p>
<p>If you work at Google and want your team to adopt AIPs for documenting how your
team does APIs, feel free to reach out to get in touch with us!</p>
<h3 id="i-have-a-question-that-isnt-answered-here-what-do-i-do">I have a question that isn't answered here. What do I do?</h3>
<p>We're still pretty new and haven't built up a long list of frequently asked
questions, so if you have a question not answered here, you can always <a href="https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/issues/new?labels=question">ask us
on GitHub</a> by filing an issue.</p>
<p>And if you already know the answer to a question that would be helpful for
others, <a href="https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/edit/master/pages/general/faq.md">send us a pull request adding it to this page</a>!</p>

  <h1 id="contributing">Contributing</h1>
<p>We'd love to accept your patches and contributions to this project.</p>
<h2 id="development-environment">Development Environment</h2>
<p>If you are contributing AIP content (rather than code) and want to be able to
view it in your browser, the easiest way to do so is to run the provided
development server.</p>
<p>We use <a href="https://pages.github.com/">GitHub Pages</a> to make this documentation available, and a specific
<a href="https://github.com/aip-dev/site-generator">site generator</a> to build the site.</p>
<p>If you have <a href="https://docker.com/">Docker</a> installed, clone this repository and run the <code>serve.sh</code>
file at the root of the repository. This script does two things:</p>
<ul>
<li>It builds the provided Docker image (unless you already have it) and tags it
  as <code>aip-site</code>.</li>
<li>It runs the <code>aip-site</code> image.</li>
</ul>
<p>The development server uses port 4000; point your web browser to
<code>http://localhost:4000</code>, and you should see the site.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> After building the Docker image for the first time, you may
experience issues if Python dependencies change underneath you. If this
happens, remove your Docker image (<code>docker rmi aip-site</code>) and run <code>serve.sh</code>
again.</p>
<h3 id="arguments">Arguments</h3>
<p>Any arguments provided to <code>serve.sh</code> (or <code>docker run</code>) are forwarded (however,
the current site generator does not honor any; this may change in the future).</p>
<h3 id="hot-reloading">Hot reloading</h3>
<p>The development server recognizes when files change (including static files)
and local changes will be automatically reflected in your browser upon reload.</p>
<h3 id="local-installation">Local Installation</h3>
<p>It is possible to run the development server locally also. The general gist of
how to do so correctly is:</p>
<ul>
<li>Install Python 3.8 if you do not already have it (direct install is fine, but
  <a href="https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv">pyenv</a> is probably the best way if you have other Python projects).</li>
<li>Create a Python 3.8 <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html">venv</a>. Once it is created, activate it in your shell
  (<code>source path/to/venv/bin/activate</code>).</li>
<li><code>pip install git+https://github.com/aip-dev/site-generator.git</code></li>
<li><code>aip-site-serve .</code></li>
</ul>
<h2 id="contributor-license-agreement">Contributor License Agreement</h2>
<p>Contributions to this project must be accompanied by a Contributor License
Agreement. You (or your employer) retain the copyright to your contribution,
this simply gives us permission to use and redistribute your contributions as
part of the project. Head over to <a href="https://cla.developers.google.com/">https://cla.developers.google.com/</a> to see
your current agreements on file or to sign a new one.</p>
<p>You generally only need to submit a CLA once, so if you have already submitted
one (even if it was for a different project), you probably do not need to do it
again.</p>
<h2 id="code-reviews">Code reviews</h2>
<p>All submissions, including submissions by project members, require review. We
use GitHub pull requests for this purpose. Consult
<a href="https://help.github.com/articles/about-pull-requests/">GitHub Help</a> for more
information on using pull requests.</p>
<h3 id="formatting">Formatting</h3>
<p>We use <a href="https://prettier.io/">prettier</a> to format Markdown, JavaScript, and (most) HTML, in order
to ensure a consistent style throughout our source. You can add prettier as a
plugin in most development environments.</p>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-1</h4>
  <h1 id="aip-purpose-and-guidelines">AIP Purpose and Guidelines</h1>
<p>As the corpus of Google APIs has grown and the API Governance team has grown to
meet the demand of supporting them, it is increasingly necessary to have a
corpus of documentation for API producers, reviewers, and other interested
parties to reference. The API style guide and introductory One Platform
documentation are intentionally terse and high-level. The AIP collection
offers a method to provide consistent documentation for API design guidance.</p>
<h2 id="what-is-an-aip">What is an AIP?</h2>
<p>AIP stands for <strong>API Improvement Proposal</strong>, which is a design document
providing high-level, concise documentation for API development. They are to
serve as the source of truth for API-related documentation at Google and the
means by which API teams discuss and come to consensus on API guidance. AIPs
are maintained as Markdown files in the <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/aip">AIP GitHub repository</a>.</p>
<h2 id="types-of-aips">Types of AIPs</h2>
<p>There are several different types of AIPs, described below. The list of AIP
types may evolve over time as necessary.</p>
<h3 id="guidance">Guidance</h3>
<p>These AIPs describe guidance on API design. These are provided as instruction
for API producers to help write simple, intuitive, and consistent APIs, and are
used by API reviewers as a basis for review comments.</p>
<h3 id="process">Process</h3>
<p>These AIPs describe a process surrounding API design. They often affect the AIP
process itself and are used to enhance the way in which AIPs are handled.</p>
<h2 id="stakeholders">Stakeholders</h2>
<p>As with any process there are many different stakeholders when it comes to
reviewing and working with AIPs. Below is a summary of the escalation path
starting with the API producer.</p>
<div class="highlight language-graphviz"><pre><span></span><code><span class="k">digraph</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nt">d_front_back</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w"></span>

<span class="p">}</span><span class="w"></span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>As noted in the diagram above, the TL is the final decision-maker on the AIP
process and the final point of escalation if necessary.</p>
<h3 id="editors">Editors</h3>
<p>The editors are the set of people who make decisions on AIPs. The general goal
is that the AIP process is collaborative and that we largely work on the basis
of consensus. However, a limited number of designated approvers is necessary,
and these Googlers will be approvers for each AIP in the general scope.</p>
<p>The list of AIP editors is currently:</p>
<ul>
<li>Angie Lin (<a href="https://github.com/alin04">@alin04</a>)</li>
<li>Jon Skeet (<a href="https://github.com/jskeet">@jskeet</a>)</li>
<li>Jose Juan Zavala Iglesias (<a href="https://github.com/itsStrobe">@itsStrobe</a>)</li>
<li>Louis Dejardin (<a href="https://github.com/loudej">@loudej</a>)</li>
<li>Noah Dietz (<a href="https://github.com/noahdietz">@noahdietz</a>)</li>
<li>Sam Levenick (<a href="https://github.com/slevenick">@slevenick</a>)</li>
<li>Sam Woodard (<a href="https://github.com/shwoodard">@shwoodard</a>)</li>
</ul>
<p>The editors are also responsible for the administrative and editorial aspects
of shepherding AIPs and managing the AIP pipeline and workflow. They approve
PRs to AIPs, assign proposal numbers, manage the agenda, set AIP states, and so
forth. They also ensure that AIPs are readable (proper spelling, grammar,
sentence structure, markup, etc.).</p>
<p>AIP editorship is by invitation of the current editors.</p>
<h2 id="domain-specific-aips">Domain-specific AIPs</h2>
<p>Some AIPs may be specific to a particular domain (for example, only to APIs
within a certain PA, or even a certain team). In this situation, the group will
be given a particular block of AIPs to use in accordance with <a href="/2">AIP-2</a>, and the
applicable AIPs will clearly indicate their scope.</p>
<h2 id="states">States</h2>
<p>At any given time, AIPs may exist in a variety of states as they work their way
through the process. The following is a summary of each state.</p>
<h3 id="draft">Draft</h3>
<p>The initial state for an AIP is the "Draft" state. This means that the AIP is
being discussed and iterated upon, primarily by the original authors. While the
editors <em>may</em> get involved at this stage, it is not necessary.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> If significant, high-level iteration is required, it is recommended
to draft AIPs in a Google doc instead of a PR. AIPs that are migrated into the
AIP system from Google Docs <strong>may</strong> skip the draft state and go directly to
reviewing provided there is sufficient approval.</p>
<h3 id="reviewing">Reviewing</h3>
<p>Once discussion on an AIP has generally concluded, but before it is formally
accepted it moves to the "Reviewing" state. This means that the authors have
reached a general consensus on the proposal and the editors are now involved.
At this stage the editors may request changes or suggest alternatives to the
proposal before moving forward.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> As a formal matter, one AIP approver (other than the author) <strong>must</strong>
provide formal signoff to advance an AIP to the reviewing state. Additionally,
there <strong>must not</strong> be formal objections ("changes requested" on the GitHub PR)
from other approvers.</p>
<h3 id="approved">Approved</h3>
<p>Once an approved AIP has been agreed upon, it enters "approved" state and is
considered "best current practice".</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> As a formal matter, two AIP approvers (other than the author)
<strong>must</strong> provide formal signoff to advance an AIP to the approved state.
Additionally, there <strong>must not</strong> be formal objections ("changes requested" on
the GitHub PR) from other approvers.</p>
<h3 id="withdrawn">Withdrawn</h3>
<p>If an AIP is withdrawn by the author or champion, it enters "withdrawn" state.
AIPs that are withdrawn may be taken up by another champion.</p>
<h3 id="rejected">Rejected</h3>
<p>If an AIP is rejected by the AIP editors, it enters "rejected" state. AIPs that
are rejected remain, and provide documentation and reference to inform future
discussions.</p>
<h3 id="deferred">Deferred</h3>
<p>If an AIP has not been acted upon for a significant period of time, the editors
may mark it as "deferred".</p>
<h3 id="replaced">Replaced</h3>
<p>If an AIP has been replaced by another AIP, it enters "replaced" state. AIP
editors are responsible to provide a notice explaining the replacement and
rationale (the replacement AIP should also clearly explain the rationale).</p>
<p>In general, API producers should rely primarily on AIPs in the "approved"
state.</p>
<h2 id="workflow">Workflow</h2>
<p>The following workflow describes the process for proposing an AIP, and moving
an AIP from proposal to implementation to final acceptance.</p>
<h3 id="overview">Overview</h3>

</code></pre></div>
<h3 id="proposing-an-aip">Proposing an AIP</h3>
<p>In order to propose an AIP, first <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/aip/issues">open an issue</a> to circulate the
fundamental idea for initial feedback. It should generally be possible to
describe the idea in a couple of pages.</p>
<p>When proposing a new AIP or changes to an existing one, it is best to reference
prior art and/or example use cases that the proposal will impact, so as to
ensure that the proposal is grounded in a realistic problem space. So, proposals
<strong>should</strong> provide concrete references and/or well-defined examples. Appropriate
material includes, but is not limited to, the following:</p>
<ul>
<li>Existing external RFCs or standards</li>
<li>A corpus of APIs that have aligned on a similar pattern e.g. <code>Search</code> methods</li>
<li>A concrete use case that has yet to be solved that exists or could exist in
  one or more APIs e.g. adding an <a href="/202">AIP-202</a> Format for <a href="/143">AIP-143</a> Unicode CLDR
  region codes</li>
</ul>
<p>Once ready, create a PR with a new file in the AIP directory using a file
titled <code>aip/new.md</code>. Ensure that the PR is editable by maintainers.</p>
<p>In most circumstances, the editors will assign the proposal an AIP number and
submit the PR with the AIP in the "Reviewing" state. The editors may reject an
AIP outright if they have an obvious reason to do so (e.g. the proposal was
already discussed and rejected in another AIP or is fundamentally unsound), in
which case the PR is not merged.</p>
<h3 id="discussing-an-aip">Discussing an AIP</h3>
<p>Once the PR is merged, the AIP author is responsible for championing the AIP on
a follow-up approval pull request. This means that the author is responsible
for pushing towards consensus around the proposal. This may involve a
discussion at the regularly scheduled meetings for the API Governance team.</p>
<p>The AIP author may modify the AIP over the course of discussion by submitting
follow-up commits to the PR.</p>
<h3 id="accepting-an-aip">Accepting an AIP</h3>
<p>The editors will work together to ensure that qualified proposals do not linger
in review.</p>
<p>To gain final approval, an AIP <strong>must</strong> be approved by, at minimum, the TL with
responsibility over the domain covered by the AIP (either design or
infrastructure) and at least one other editor, with no editors actively
requesting changes.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> If an AIP editor is the primary author of an AIP, then at least two
<em>other</em> editors must approve it.</p>
<p>Once the AIP is approved, the editors will update the state of the AIP to
reflect this and submit the PR.</p>
<h3 id="withdrawing-or-rejecting-an-aip">Withdrawing or Rejecting an AIP</h3>
<p>The author of an AIP may decide, after further consideration, that an AIP
should not advance. If so, the author may withdraw the AIP by updating the PR
adding a notice of withdrawal with an explanation of the rationale.
Additionally, the author may be unable to get consensus among the group and the
AIP editors may elect to reject the AIP. In this situation, the AIP editors
shall amend the PR adding a notice of rejection with an explanation of the
rationale. In both cases, the AIP editors update the state accordingly and
submit the PR.</p>
<h3 id="replacing-an-aip">Replacing an AIP</h3>
<p>In rare cases, it may be necessary to replace an AIP with another one. This is
not general practice: minor edits to approved AIPs are acceptable, and will be
the common way to tweak guidance. However, if new guidance fundamentally alters
the old guidance in some way, then the AIP editors shall create a new AIP that,
once approved, will replace the old one. The old one then enters "Replaced"
state, and will link to the new, current AIP.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2025-01-09</strong>: Add requirement to include references/examples in proposals.</li>
<li><strong>2024-09-04</strong>: Updated names of current editors and remove TLs.</li>
<li><strong>2023-05-10</strong>: Updated names of current and editors and TLs.</li>
<li><strong>2019-07-30</strong>: Further clarified AIP quorum requirements.</li>
<li><strong>2019-05-12</strong>: Collapsed AIP approvers and editors into a single position,
  relaxed approval rules from full quorum.</li>
<li><strong>2019-05-04</strong>: Updated the AIP to refer to GitHub processes, rather than
  internal processes.</li>
</ul>

        Adopting AIPs in your company
      </li>
    </ol>
  </nav>
</section>
  <h1 id="adopting-aips-in-your-company">Adopting AIPs in your company</h1>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> We're working on some tooling to make this better. Keep an eye on
<a href="https://github.com/googleapis/aip/issues/98">this GitHub issue</a> for progress.</p>
<p>While AIPs originated at Google and were aimed for Googlers writing Google
APIs, much of the guidance documented is useful outside of Google. This
document describes how you might adopt AIPs as the way you document your own
APIs even if you don't work at Google.</p>
<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Sometimes private organizations might have API guidance that they don't want or
care to share with the rest of the world. For example, maybe in your company
(let's say, Acme, Inc), you identify your resources with a special field called
<code>string acme_id</code>.</p>
<p>This rule could be written as an AIP, but there's no reason to share this rule
with everyone -- it's only for you and your development team. However, you
don't want this to conflict with a future AIP (e.g., if you make this AIP-1234,
maybe that AIP will get written in the future and then you'll have a conflict).
So what do you do?</p>
<h2 id="the-9000-block">The 9000 block</h2>
<p>Much like the Unicode specification, we've reserved the 9000 block of AIP
numbers (that is, AIP-9000 through AIP-9999) to be for "internal use". This
means that these AIPs will never have public documentation and are free for
private companies to use for their own API guidance. As a result, all you have
to do is write your AIPs as usual and give them a number in the 9000 block.</p>
<h2 id="custom-aip-domains">Custom AIP domains</h2>
<p>We're working on a separate fork-able repository that you can copy and use as
your 9000 block AIP repository. The page rendered by GitHub Pages will serve
only the AIPs in that block and redirect all other pages to [aip.dev][].</p>
<p>In short, this means that you can create your own AIP domain (e.g.,
<code>aip.example.com</code>) and point that to the forked GitHub repository which will
redirect for all well-known AIPs and serve all internal AIPs from your own
repository. Once you've done that, you can cite all AIPs specifically using
that domain name (e.g., <code>aip.example.com/1234</code>) and you'll always get sent to
the right place.</p>
<h2 id="forking-aip">Forking AIP</h2>
<p>You can fork the AIP project and run it in your own domain if necessary. This
will allow you to customize the AIPs to your organization's needs. Or you could
use the infrastructure to create your own set of AIPs.</p>
<h3 id="updating-the-url">Updating the URL</h3>
<p>To run the AIP infrastructure as a GitHub Page in a another repository, the
<code>_config.yaml</code> file must be updated to work correctly in the new repo.</p>
<p>If a new custom domain and CNAME have been created for your AIP, only the <code>url</code>
property will need to be updated to the new domain.</p>
<div class="highlight language-None"><pre><span></span><code>url: https://aip.dev
</code></pre></div>
<p>If you are not creating a new domain, it will be necessary to add the <code>baseurl</code>
property to the <code>_config.yaml</code>. This property should contain any additional
path information that may be appended to the domain in the <code>url</code>.</p>
<p>For example, assume GitHub user jdoe123 forked the aip project into a
repository named my-aips. If this user served the content from their master
branch, the url to the GitHub pages would be
<code>https://jdoe123.github.io/my-aips/</code>. The accompanying <code>_config.yaml</code> would be
configured as follows:</p>
<div class="highlight language-None"><pre><span></span><code>url: https://jdoe123.github.io
baseurl: /my-aips
</code></pre></div>
<p>For more information about about how these values are used by GitHub Pages, see
the <a href="https://jekyllrb.com/news/2016/10/06/jekyll-3-3-is-here/#2-relative_url-and-absolute_url-filters">release notes</a> that standardized these configurations in Jekyll.</p>
<h3 id="configuring-navigation">Configuring Navigation</h3>
<p>The navigation headers and bar are generated dynamically based on the
<code>_data/header.yaml</code> and <code>_data/nav.yaml</code> files respectively.</p>
<p>The schema for the navigation bar can be viewed under
<code>assets/schemas/nav-schema.yaml</code>. It supports two types of navigation
components; <code>static_group</code> and <code>matter_group</code>. A <code>static_group</code> menu component
will always show the same navigation elements, regardless of the content of the
page and the repository. A <code>matter_group</code> component is generated dynamically
based on the AIPs in the domain, or the current page in the site. The
configurations for a <code>matter_group</code> can be viewed in the
<code>assets/schemas/nav-components.yaml#defintions/matter_group</code> schema.</p>
<p>The header is just a specially rendered <code>static_group</code> component. The schema
can be viewed at <code>assets/schemas/static_group.yaml</code>.</p>
<h3 id="testing-configuration">Testing Configuration</h3>
<p>The <code>tests</code> folder contains an npm test module that will validate your data
files. Running these tests requires npm and mocha. Once these are installed
that tests can be ran with the <code>npm test</code> command.</p>

  <h1 id="content-licensing">Content licensing</h1>
<p>We are pleased to license much of the AIP content under terms that explicitly
encourage people to take, modify, reuse, re-purpose, and remix our work as they
see fit.</p>
<p>You will find the following notice at the bottom of many pages:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Except as otherwise noted, the content of this page is licensed under the
<a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License</a>, and code samples are
licensed under the <a href="https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0">Apache 2.0 License</a>. For details, see
<a href="./licensing.md">content licensing</a>.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>When you see a page with this notice you are free to use
<a href="#restrictions">nearly everything</a> on the page in your own creations. For
example, you could quote the text in a book, cut-and-paste sections to your
blog, record it as an audiobook for the visually impaired, or even translate it
into Swahili. Really. That's what open content licenses are all about. We just
ask that you give us <a href="#attribution">attribution</a> when you reuse our work.</p>
<p>In addition, you are free to use the computer source code that appears in the
content (such as in examples) in the code of your own projects.</p>
<h2 id="restrictions">Restrictions</h2>
<p>We say "nearly everything" as there are a few simple conditions that apply.</p>
<p>Google's trademarks and other brand features are not included in this license.
Please see our <a href="http://www.google.com/permissions/guidelines.html">standard guidelines for third party use of Google brand
features</a> for information about this usage.</p>
<p>In some cases, a page may include content consisting of images, audio or video
material, or a link to content on a different webpage (such as videos or slide
decks). This content is not covered by the license, unless specifically noted.</p>
<h2 id="attribution">Attribution</h2>
<p>Proper attribution is required when you reuse or create modified versions of
content that appears on a page made available under the terms of the Creative
Commons Attribution license. The complete requirements for attribution can be
found in section 3 of the <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode">Creative Commons legal code</a>.</p>
<p>In practice we ask that you provide attribution to Google to the best of the
ability of the medium in which you are producing the work.</p>
<p>There are several typical ways in which this might apply:</p>
<h3 id="exact-reproductions">Exact reproductions</h3>
<p>If your online work <em>exactly reproduces</em> text or images from this site, in
whole or in part, please include a paragraph at the bottom of your page that
reads:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Portions of this page are reproduced from work created and <a href="./licensing.md">shared by
Google</a> and used according to terms described in the <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">Creative
Commons 4.0 Attribution License</a>.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Also, please link back to the original source page so that readers can refer to
it for more information.</p>
<h3 id="modified-versions">Modified versions</h3>
<p>If your online work shows modified text or images based on the content from
this site, please include a paragraph at the bottom of your page that reads:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Portions of this page are modifications based on work created and <a href="./licensing.md">shared by
Google</a> and used according to terms described in the <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">Creative
Commons 4.0 Attribution License</a>.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Again, please link back to the original source page so that readers can refer
to it for more information. This is even more important when the content has
been modified.</p>
<h3 id="other-media">Other media</h3>
<p>If you produce non-hypertext works, such as books, audio, or video, we ask that
you make a best effort to include a spoken or written attribution in the spirit
of the messages above.</p>

Last updated: May 13, 2019</p></footer>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-2</h4>
  <h1 id="aip-numbering">AIP Numbering</h1>
<p>The AIP system provides a mechanism to index and have a single source of truth
for API Improvement Proposals, as well as iterate on them collaboratively and
transparently.</p>
<p>This document describes the AIP numbering system.</p>
<h2 id="assigning-aip-numbers">Assigning AIP Numbers</h2>
<p>The AIP editors (see <a href="/1">AIP-1</a>) are responsible for assigning a number
to each AIP when it is accepted as a draft for review. Importantly, <em>all</em> AIPs
have numbers, not just approved ones. The <a href="/">AIP Index</a> clearly delineates
which AIPs are approved and binding and which are under discussion.</p>
<p>The editors may decide to reserve a specific block of numbers for groups of
AIPs that are related in some way (for example, that are only scoped to a
specific subset of APIs).</p>
<p>Beyond this, AIP numbers are assigned arbitrarily. In general, the editors will
take the next AIP number off of the stack to assign to a draft AIP, but
occasionally may use a special/joke number if useful for mnemonic or other
reasons.</p>
<h2 id="aip-blocks">AIP Blocks</h2>
<p>Currently recognized blocks of AIP numbers are:</p>
<h3 id="generally-applicable">Generally Applicable</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>1-99:</strong> Reserved for meta-AIPs (generally process-related).</li>
<li><strong>100-999:</strong> General API design guidance</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="google-product-areas">Google Product Areas</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>2700-2799:</strong> Apps (Google Workspace)</li>
<li><strong>2500-2599:</strong> Cloud</li>
<li><strong>3000-3099:</strong> Actions on Google</li>
<li><strong>3200-3299:</strong> Firebase</li>
<li><strong>4100-4199:</strong> Auth libraries</li>
<li><strong>4200-4299:</strong> Client libraries</li>
<li><strong>4600-4699:</strong> Geo</li>
</ul>
<p>To request a block for a specific team that is publishing API guidance or
documentation germane to that specific team, reach out to api-editors@.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2019-10-03:</strong> The 3000-3099 block was assigned to Actions on Google.</li>
<li><strong>2019-01-26:</strong> The general API design guidance block was expanded to include
  100-199.</li>
<li><strong>2018-10-24:</strong> The 4600-4699 block was assigned to Google Geo.</li>
<li><strong>2018-10-02:</strong> The 2500-2599 block was assigned to Google Cloud Platform.</li>
<li><strong>2018-10-02:</strong> The 2700-2799 block was assigned to Google Workspace.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-3</h4>
  <h1 id="aip-versioning">AIP Versioning</h1>
<p>This AIP defines the versioning scheme of the AIPs.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<ul>
<li>The AIPs <strong>must</strong> be versioned by date, using the <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime">ISO-8601 format of
  <code>YYYY-MM-DD</code></a>, that corresponds to the
  date the version was added.</li>
<li>AIPs versions <strong>must</strong> be available as a tag on the source control system used
  to store the AIPs, of the format <code>v{version}</code>. Example: <code>v2023-03-28</code>.</li>
<li>The AIPs <strong>must</strong> have a new version when there is a significant change to one
  or more AIPs.</li>
<li>Each AIP <strong>must</strong> include a changelog section, with the date the change was
  made and a short description.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="rationale">Rationale</h2>
<p>Versions serve as reference points to AIPs at a specific point in time. They are
crucial since guidance on an AIP can be reversed, or include significant changes
such that they are no longer similar to the original design. APIs using AIPs may
need to reference older AIP guidance to justify their design choice.</p>
<h3 id="rationale-for-date-based-versioning">Rationale for date-based versioning</h3>
<p>With date-based versioning, a client can easily find the AIP guidance at the
time an API was authored.</p>
<h3 id="why-not-individually-versioned-aips">Why not individually versioned AIPs</h3>
<p>An alternative to a universal version is to have specific versions attached to
each AIP.</p>
<p>AIPs often cross-reference one another. If each AIP had a specific version, then
cross-references would also have to specify specific versions of those
referenced AIPs to provide complete guidance.</p>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-8</h4>
  <h1 id="aip-style-and-guidance">AIP Style and Guidance</h1>
<p>AIP stands for <strong>API Improvement Proposal</strong>, which is a design document
providing high-level, concise documentation for API design and development. The
goal is for these documents to serve as the source of truth for API-related
documentation at Google and the way API teams discuss and come to consensus on
API guidance.</p>
<p>AIPs are most useful when they are clear and concise, and cover a single topic
or inquiry well. In the same way that AIPs describe consistent patterns and
style for use in APIs, they also <em>follow</em> consistent patterns and style.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<ul>
<li>AIPs <strong>must</strong> cover a single, discrete topic, and provide clear, actionable
  guidance.</li>
<li>AIPs <strong>must not</strong> duplicate or contradict guidance in another AIP.</li>
<li>AIPs <strong>may</strong> also cover what <em>not</em> to do, but <strong>should not</strong> cover <em>only</em>
  anti-patterns.</li>
<li>If AIP guidance is conditional (e.g. a design pattern such as Jobs), the
  guidance <strong>must</strong> clearly explain under what conditions the guidance should be
  followed.</li>
</ul>
<p>Guidance contained within an AIP <strong>must</strong> be beneficial to one or more
types of clients or their authors, including but not limited to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Asset inventories which can be used to audit and analyze resources.</li>
<li>Command line interfaces for exploration and simple automation.</li>
<li>Custom controllers (e.g. auto-scalers) which poll live state and adjust
  resource configuration accordingly.</li>
<li><a href="/9#iac">IaC</a> clients for orchestration and automation of multiple resources.</li>
<li>Recommendation tools which provide guidance on which APIs are useful for
  specific use cases, and how to use them.</li>
<li>SDKs to interact with an API from a programming language, often used heavily
  for data-plane operations.</li>
<li>Security orchestration, automation, and remediation tools.</li>
<li>Simple scripts to automate or orchestrate tasks.</li>
<li>Test frameworks.</li>
<li>Tools that operate on resource data at rest.</li>
<li>Visual User Interfaces for visualization and one-off manual actions.</li>
<li>Users.</li>
</ul>
<p>Examples of improvements include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Requiring new proto annotations that enable more descriptive interfaces on
  clients (e.g. requiring <code>singular</code> and <code>plural</code> on a <code>google.api.resource</code>
  annotation).</li>
</ul>
<p>AIP guidance <strong>must not</strong> be a significant detriment to a client's usability or
implementation difficulty, or maintenance difficulty.</p>
<p>Examples of detriments include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Introduction of a non-uniform pattern in a standard method such that all
  clients must introduce additional code without sufficient benefit (e.g. List
  behaves like this <em>except</em> for resources that start with the name Foo).</li>
<li>Renames of well-established fields for minor improvements in readability (e.g.
  rename <code>expire_time</code> to <code>lapse_time</code> since <code>lapse</code> is a common term in my
  service).</li>
</ul>
<p>While the length of AIPs will necessarily vary based on the complexity of the
question, most AIPs <strong>should</strong> be able to cover their content in roughly two
printed pages.</p>
<h3 id="file-structure">File structure</h3>
<p>AIPs <strong>must</strong> be written in Markdown, and <strong>must</strong> be named using their
four-digit number (example: <code>0008.md</code>). AIPs that serve a specific scope
<strong>must</strong> be in the subdirectory for that scope.</p>
<p>AIPs <strong>must</strong> have appropriate front matter.</p>
<div class="highlight language-yaml"><pre><span></span><code><span class="nn">---</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nt">id</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">8</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nt">state</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">reviewing</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nt">created</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">2019-05-28</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nt">permalink</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">/8</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nt">redirect_from</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p p-Indicator">-</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">/08</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p p-Indicator">-</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">/008</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p p-Indicator">-</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="l l-Scalar l-Scalar-Plain">/0008</span><span class="w"></span>
<span class="nn">---</span><span class="w"></span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>Front matter for AIPs <strong>must</strong> include:</p>
<ul>
<li>The <code>aip</code> key:<ul>
<li><code>id</code>: Required. The ID for the given AIP, as an integer.</li>
<li><code>state</code>: Required. The current state of the AIP, in all lower-case. The
  valid states are listed in <a href="/1">AIP-1</a>, and common states are <code>draft</code>,
  <code>reviewing</code>, and <code>approved</code>.</li>
<li><code>created</code>: Required. The ISO-8601 date (<code>yyyy-mm-dd</code>) when the AIP was
  originally drafted, with no quotes.</li>
<li><code>updated</code>: The ISO-8601 date (<code>yyyy-mm-dd</code>) when the AIP was last revised.</li>
<li><code>scope</code>: The scope for the AIP. This <strong>must</strong> match the directory name for
  that scope. Required for AIPs with IDs &gt;= 1000, prohibited otherwise.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The <code>permalink</code> key (required): This <strong>must</strong> be set to
  <code>/{aip.scope}/{aip.id}</code>. If there is no scope, use <code>/{aip.id}</code> instead.</li>
<li>The <code>redirect_from</code> key: This should include a list of any <code>/{aip.id}</code>
  permutations that a reader would be likely to enter, including:<ul>
<li><code>/{aip.id}</code> (for AIPs where the permalink includes the scope)</li>
<li>AIP IDs with zero-padding, for each level of zero-padding up to four digits
  (for example: <code>/08</code>, <code>/008</code>, <code>/0008</code>).</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="document-structure">Document structure</h3>
<p>AIPs <strong>must</strong> begin with a top-level heading with the AIP's title (<code># Title</code>).
The title <strong>should</strong> be a noun (not an imperative). For example, "Bad API
precedents" not "Avoid breaking API precedent".</p>
<p>AIPs <strong>should</strong> then begin with an introduction (with no additional heading),
followed by a <code>## Guidance</code> heading. If necessary, the AIP <strong>may</strong> include any
of the following after the guidance, in the following order:</p>
<ul>
<li>"Further reading" is a bulleted list of links to other AIPs that are useful to
  fully understand the current AIP.</li>
<li>"Appendices" covering further explanation in the same AIP. These are
  relatively rare but are important in cases where an AIP requires a lot of
  justification for the decision. Often this is primarily an explanation of
  alternatives considered to help explain the guidance.</li>
<li>"Changelog" is a bulleted list of changes made to the AIP since the first
  writing.</li>
</ul>
<p>The guidance section <strong>may</strong> include subsections that elaborate further on
details. Subsections will automatically create an entry in the table of
contents, and an anchor for citations.</p>
<p>Below is an example AIP shell that uses each major section:</p>
<div class="highlight language-md"><pre><span></span><code><span class="gh"># AIP title</span>

The introductory text explains the background and reason why the AIP exists. It
lays out the basic question, but does not tell the reader what to do.

<span class="gu">## Guidance</span>

The &quot;guidance&quot; section helps the reader know what to do. A common format for
the guidance section is a high-level imperative, followed by an example,
followed by a bulleted list explaining the example.

<span class="gu">### Subsection</span>

Individual subsections can be cited individually, and further elaborate
details.

<span class="gu">## Rationale</span>

The &quot;rationale&quot; section is optional, and helps the reader understand the
motivation behind specific guidance within the AIP.

Deeper explanations of design justification and tradeoffs <span class="gs">**must**</span> be in the
rationale instead of other sections, to ensure the rest of the document acts as
an easily actionable reference.

<span class="gu">## History</span>

The &quot;history&quot; section is optional, and documents events and context around a
significant edit to an AIP. For example, explanation of rewrite would be
included in this section

While the changelog is a dotted list of one-line summaries of changes to an AIP,
the history section should elaborate on significant events in a descriptive
format.

The section <span class="gs">**must not**</span> be used to exhaustively enumerate all changes. This
is what the changelog provides.

<span class="gu">## Further reading</span>

A bulleted list of (usually) other AIPs, in the following format:

<span class="k">-</span> [<span class="nt">AIP-1</span>](<span class="na">/1</span>): AIP purpose and guidelines

<span class="gu">## Changelog</span>

A bulleted list of changes in reverse chronological order, using the following
format:

<span class="k">-</span> <span class="gs">**2020-02-18**</span>: Specified ordering.
<span class="k">-</span> <span class="gs">**2019-07-01**</span>: Added a subsection clarifying XYZ.
</code></pre></div>
<p>AIPs <strong>should</strong> attempt to follow this overall format if possible, but AIPs
<strong>may</strong> deviate from it if necessary (in particular, if the AIP would be more
difficult to understand, even for a reader already accustomed to reading AIPs in
the usual format).</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Except for the title, AIPs <strong>must</strong> only use the second heading level
(<code>##</code>) and above. AIPs <strong>should</strong> only use the second and third heading levels
(<code>##</code>, <code>###</code>).</p>
<h3 id="requirement-keywords">Requirement keywords</h3>
<p>AIPs <strong>should</strong> use the following requirement level keywords: "MUST", "MUST
NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", and "MAY", which are to be interpreted as
described in <a href="https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt">RFC 2119</a>.</p>
<p>When using these terms in AIPs, they <strong>must</strong> be lower-case and <strong>bold</strong>. These
terms <strong>should not</strong> be used in other ways.</p>
<p>If "SHOULD" or "SHOULD NOT" are used, they <strong>must</strong> include valid examples of
where other concerns may override the guidance.</p>
<p><strong>Important:</strong> If rationale is used, it exists to provide background and a more
complete understanding, but <strong>must not</strong> contain guidance (and RFC-2119 terms
<strong>must not</strong> be used).</p>
<h3 id="code-examples">Code examples</h3>
<p>API design examples in AIPs <strong>should</strong> use <a href="https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/">protocol buffers</a>. Examples
<strong>should</strong> cover only enough syntax to explain the concept. When using RPCs in
examples, a <code>google.api.http</code> annotation <strong>should</strong> be included.</p>
<h3 id="referencing-aips">Referencing AIPs</h3>
<p>When AIPs reference other AIPs, the prosaic text <strong>must</strong> use the format
<code>AIP-XXXX</code> without zero-padding (e.g., <code>[AIP-8](/8)</code>, not <code>[AIP-0008](/0008)</code>), and <strong>must</strong>
link to the relevant AIP. AIP links <strong>may</strong> point to a particular section of the
AIP if appropriate.</p>
<p><strong>Important:</strong> AIP links <strong>must</strong> use the relative path to the file in the
repository (such as <code>/8</code> for core AIPs, or <code>/8</code> for AIPs in a
subdirectory); this ensures that the link works both on the AIP site, when
viewing the Markdown file on GitHub, using the local development server, or a
branch.</p>
<h2 id="rationale">Rationale</h2>
<h3 id="designing-for-a-broad-set-of-clients">Designing for a broad set of clients</h3>
<p>API guidance, similar to any software, is most beneficial when there is a clear
purpose and target beneficiary.</p>
<p>The beneficiaries of improved API design are users. These users interact with
APIs via a variety of clients, depending on their use case as enumerated above.</p>
<p>API guidance must in turn consider the impact broadly across these clients.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2023-05-20</strong>: Increase API guidance scope to include broad set of clients.</li>
<li><strong>2023-03-30</strong>: Removed appendix, added rationale and history to the template.</li>
<li><strong>2020-02-18</strong>: Specified reverse chronological ordering for changelog items.</li>
<li><strong>2019-08-23</strong>: Added guidance for internal AIP links.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-9</h4>
  <h1 id="glossary">Glossary</h1>
<p>In the name of brevity, this AIP defines some common terminology here rather
than in each AIP individually.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>The following terminology <strong>should</strong> be used consistently throughout AIPs.</p>
<h3 id="api">API</h3>
<p>Application programming interface. This can be a local interface (such as a
client library) or a Network API (defined below).</p>
<h3 id="api-backend">API backend</h3>
<p>A set of servers and related infrastructure that implements the business logic
for an API service. An individual API backend server is often called an API
server.</p>
<h3 id="api-consumer">API consumer</h3>
<p>The entity that consumes an API service. For Google APIs, it typically is a
Google project that owns the client application or the server resource.</p>
<h3 id="api-definition">API definition</h3>
<p>The definition of an API, usually defined in a Protocol Buffer service. An API
definition can be implemented by any number of API services.</p>
<h3 id="api-frontend">API frontend</h3>
<p>A set of servers plus related infrastructure that provides common functionality
across API services, such as load balancing and authentication. An individual
API frontend server is often called an API proxy.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> the API frontend and the API backend may run next to each other or far
away from each other. In some cases, they can be compiled into a single
application binary and run inside a single process.</p>
<h3 id="api-interface">API interface</h3>
<p>The element of an API specification IDL that groups API methods, such as a
Protocol Buffers <code>service</code> definition. It is typically mapped to a similar high
level grouping mechanism in most programming languages, like a <code>class</code> or
<code>interface</code>.</p>
<h3 id="api-method">API method</h3>
<p>An individual operation within an API. It is typically represented in Protocol
Buffers by an <code>rpc</code> definition, and is mapped to a function in the API in most
programming languages.</p>
<h3 id="api-producer">API producer</h3>
<p>The entity that produces an API service. For Google APIs, it typically is a
Google team responsible for the API service.</p>
<h3 id="api-product">API product</h3>
<p>An API service and its related components, such as Terms of Service,
documentation, client libraries, and service support, are collectively presented
to customers as a API product. For example, Google Calendar API.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> people sometimes refer to an API product simply as an API.</p>
<h3 id="api-service">API service</h3>
<p>A deployed implementation of one or more APIs, exposed on one or more network
addresses, such as the Cloud Pub/Sub API.</p>
<h3 id="api-service-definition">API service definition</h3>
<p>The combination of API definitions (<code>.proto</code> files) and API service
configurations (<code>.yaml</code> files) used to define an API service. The schema for
Google API service definition is <code>google.api.Service</code>.</p>
<h3 id="api-service-endpoint">API service endpoint</h3>
<p>Refers to a network address that an API service uses to handle incoming API
requests. One API service may have multiple API service endpoints, such as
<code>https://pubsub.googleapis.com</code> and <code>https://content-pubsub.googleapis.com</code>.</p>
<h3 id="api-service-name">API service name</h3>
<p>Refers to the logical identifier of an API service. Google APIs use RFC 1035 DNS
compatible names as their API service names, such as <code>pubsub.googleapis.com</code>.</p>
<h3 id="api-title">API title</h3>
<p>Refers to the user-facing product title of an API service, such as "Cloud Pub/Sub
API".</p>
<h3 id="api-request">API request</h3>
<p>A single invocation of an API method. It is often used as the unit for billing,
logging, monitoring, and rate limiting.</p>
<h3 id="api-version">API version</h3>
<p>The version of an API or a group of APIs if they are defined together. An API
version is often represented by a string, such as "v1", and presents in API
requests and Protocol Buffers package names.</p>
<h3 id="client">Client</h3>
<p>Clients are programs that perform a specific tasks by calling an API or generic
tools, such as CLIs, that expose the API in a user-accessible fashion or operate
on resource data at rest.</p>
<p>Examples of clients include the following:</p>
<ul>
<li>Command line interfaces</li>
<li>Libraries, such as an SDK for a particular programming language</li>
<li>Scripts that operates on a JSON representation of a resource after reading it
  from an API</li>
<li>Tools, such as a <a href="#declarative-clients">Declarative clients</a></li>
<li>Visual UIs, such as a web application</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="google-api">Google API</h3>
<p>A Network API exposed by a Google service. Most of these are hosted on the
<code>googleapis.com</code> domain. It does not include other types of APIs, such as client
libraries and SDKs.</p>
<h3 id="declarative-clients">Declarative Clients</h3>
<p>Declarative Clients, also known as Infrastructure as Code (IaC), describes a
category of clients that consumes a markup language or code that represents
resources exposed by an API, and executes the appropriate imperative actions to
drive the resource to that desired state. To determine what changes to make and
if a set of updates was successful a declarative client compares server side
resource attributes with client defined values. The comparison feature ensures
accuracy of a creation or an update but it requires services to treat the client
set fields as read-only and diligently preserve those values.</p>
<p>Examples of complexities that declarative clients abstract away include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Determining the appropriate imperative action (create / update / delete) to
  achieve desired state.</li>
<li>Ordering of these imperative actions.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://www.terraform.io/">Terraform</a> is an example of such a client.</p>
<h3 id="user">User</h3>
<p>A human being which is using an API directly, such as with cURL. This term is
defined to differentiate usage in the AIPs between a human <em>user</em> and a
programmatic <em>client</em>.</p>
<h3 id="network-api">Network API</h3>
<p>An API that operates across a network of computers. Network APIs communicate
using network protocols including HTTP, and are frequently produced by
organizations separate from those that consume them.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2025-08-13</strong>: Add API inteface entry</li>
<li><strong>2024-12-18</strong>: Downcase headings and terms as per dev docs style</li>
<li><strong>2024-10-23</strong>: Add API Title entry</li>
<li><strong>2023-07-24</strong>: Rename IaC to Declarative Clients</li>
<li><strong>2023-04-01</strong>: Adding definition of IaC</li>
<li><strong>2023-03-24</strong>: Reformatting content to include anchor links.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-100</h4>
  <h1 id="api-design-review-faq">API Design Review FAQ</h1>
<p>API design review exists to ensure a simple, intuitive, and consistent API
experience throughout our API corpus.</p>
<h2 id="do-i-need-api-design-approval">Do I need API design approval?</h2>
<p><strong>TL;DR:</strong> You usually need API design approval if you are launching an API
that users can code against (either now or in the future) at the beta or GA
quality level.</p>
<p>API design review is fundamentally about ensuring we provide a simple and
consistent experience for our users, and therefore is only expected for APIs
that users code directly against.</p>
<p>The following flowchart illustrates whether or not your API needs to go through
the design review process:</p>

<h3 id="who-should-code-directly-against-it">Who should code directly against it?</h3>
<p>One of the more complex questions is, "Who should code directly against this
API?" API design review is primarily concerned about the API's audience. This
means we care about who is permitted to write their own HTTP/gRPC calls against
the service, and who is able to see the documentation. (We do <em>not</em> care about
questions such as whether the service is exposed on the public network.)</p>
<p>Design review is expected if the general public is intended to read
documentation and write code that interacts with the service.</p>
<p>The following situations <strong>do not</strong> require design review:</p>
<ul>
<li>An API which will only ever be used by Googlers, or internal tools (for
  example, Pantheon).</li>
<li>An API which will only ever be called by an executable program released by
  Google (even if the API could be reverse-engineered from the executable).</li>
<li>An API which will only ever be called by a single customer or small set of
  customers under contract, and which will <em>never</em> be made more widely
  available. (Design review is still recommended in this case, but not
  required.)</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="alpha">Alpha</h3>
<p>For alpha, API design review is optional but recommended. It may often make
sense to endeavor to get initial feedback from customers quickly, and launching
an alpha can be a way of gaining data to determine the best answer to some
usability questions; therefore, bypassing review may be expedient. On the other
hand, launching an alpha requires building an implementation which then takes
engineering effort to update if the API design review at the beta stage raises
concerns. Because API design review can precede implementation work, we
recommend a design review for alpha.</p>
<h2 id="why-is-design-review-important">Why is design review important?</h2>
<p><strong>TL;DR:</strong> Product excellence.</p>
<p>Our design review process exists to ensure that the APIs that we present to
customers are <strong>simple</strong>, <strong>intuitive</strong>, and <strong>consistent</strong>. Your reviewer
approaches your API from the standpoint of a naïve user, thinks through the
resources and actions that your API provides, and attempts to make the surface
as accessible and extensible as possible.</p>
<p>Your design reviewer is not only evaluating your API, but also checking to
ensure that your API is consistent with Google's existing corpus of APIs. Many
customers use multiple APIs, and therefore it is important that our conventions
and naming choices line up with customer expectations.</p>
<h2 id="what-should-i-expect">What should I expect?</h2>
<h3 id="how-long-does-the-review-process-take">How long does the review process take?</h3>
<p>Reviewers make an effort to keep up with their assigned reviews and offer
feedback frequently, so as not to cause unnecessary delay, but it's generally
best to begin the review process early in case there are delays.</p>
<p>The design review process varies based on the size and complexity of the
underlying API surface:</p>
<ul>
<li>Incremental changes to existing APIs generally take a few days.</li>
<li>Small APIs usually take around a week.</li>
<li>Entirely new APIs with large surfaces tend to take no less than a week. In
  cases with extraordinarily large surfaces (e.g., Cloud AutoML), reviews may
  take a month or more to go through design review.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="how-do-reviewers-approach-my-api">How do reviewers approach my API?</h3>
<p>API reviewers seek to approach your API the same way that your users will, by
focusing primarily on the API surface and its user-facing documentation. In an
ideal world, your API reviewer will ask the types of design questions that
users will ask (and nudge the API toward raising fewer of those questions in
the first place).</p>
<h3 id="what-is-precedent">What is precedent?</h3>
<p>In general, we want Google APIs to be as consistent as possible. Once customers
learn their first Google API, it should be easier to learn the second (and then
the third, and so on) because we are using the same patterns consistently.</p>
<p>We refer to <strong>precedent</strong> to mean decisions that have already been made by
previous APIs, which generally should be binding upon newer APIs in similar
situations. The most common example of this is naming: we have a list of
<a href="https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/standard_fields">standard fields</a> that dictate how we use common terms like <code>name</code>,
<code>create_time</code>, and so forth, and which also dictates that we always attach <em>the
same</em> name to the same concept.</p>
<p>Precedent also applies to <em>patterns</em>. All APIs should implement pagination the
same way. Ditto for long-running operations, import and export, and so on. Once
a pattern has been established, we seek to implement that pattern the same way
wherever it is germane.</p>
<h2 id="what-should-i-do">What should I do?</h2>
<h3 id="if-i-have-a-launch-on-a-tight-deadline">...if I have a launch on a tight deadline?</h3>
<p>The best thing that you can do is to engage design review as early as possible.
Additionally, make your reviewers aware of your timeline so that they are
aware, and can endeavor to provide you the best possible service. We <em>want</em> you
to make your deadline if at all possible.</p>
<p>For time-sensitive <em>alpha</em> launches, an API <strong>may</strong> launch without receiving
design review approval. Such launches <strong>must</strong> be limited to a known set of
users. In this case, the reviewers will provide notes for the API team to take
under consideration for subsequent stages.</p>
<p><strong>Warning:</strong> Launching an API in alpha with an incomplete design review <strong>does
not</strong> enshrine that API's decisions. Design review will be required to promote
the API to beta, and API reviewers will block your beta launch if there are
issues.</p>
<p>For launch stages after alpha, the API design review is mandatory due to its
impact on user experience across the board. Your team's inconsistencies affect
more than just your team.</p>
<p>In some cases, there is a difficult choice to be made between product
excellence and either engineering effort or deadlines. These are difficult
business decisions and we understand that they are sometimes necessary;
however, a director or VP must make an explicit choice to put these other
concerns ahead of product excellence when choosing to bypass design review or
disregard reviewers' feedback.</p>
<h3 id="to-make-my-review-go-faster">...to make my review go faster?</h3>
<p>A few tips:</p>
<ul>
<li>Begin API review as early as possible, and follow up frequently.</li>
<li>Run the <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/api-linter">API linter</a> beforehand. (If you are disabling the linter at any
  point, explain why. Reviewers often find that the linter is disabled because
  it did its job.)</li>
<li>Ensure that every message, RPC, and field is <em>usefully</em> commented. Comments
  should be in valid American English and say something meaningful.</li>
<li>If your API reviewer asks you to explain something, add the explanation <em>in
  the proto comments</em>, rather than the code review conversation. This will very
  often save you a round trip.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="if-one-of-my-api-reviewers-is-unresponsive">...if one of my API reviewers is unresponsive?</h3>
<p>Reach out to the reviewer on Chat. If that fails, reach out to the other
reviewer, who will coordinate accordingly. If that fails also, escalate
according to <a href="/1">AIP-1</a>.</p>
<h3 id="if-i-have-a-design-question">...if I have a design question?</h3>
<p>The first places to look at the <a href="https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/">API style guide</a>, the <a href="/">AIP index</a>, and
other public APIs within Google. Other public APIs are particularly valuable;
it is common that someone has encountered a situation that is germane to your
question.</p>
<h3 id="if-i-have-a-question-not-covered-there">...if I have a question not covered there?</h3>
<p>Reach out to api-design@google.com with your question.</p>
<p>This generally works best when you are seeking guidance on a specific question
related to API design, and when you clearly explain your use case and provide
examples.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> The membership of this list comprises almost exclusively volunteers,
who spend the majority of their time doing something else. We do our best to be
responsive, but please be patient with us.</p>
<h3 id="if-a-question-is-complex-and-languishing-in-a-cl">...if a question is complex and languishing in a CL?</h3>
<p>While the code review interface is the best way to resolve questions when
practical, sometimes there are issues that are sufficiently complicated that
working them out in the code review tool is not feasible. In this situation,
reach out to your reviewers and ask to schedule a meeting. In general, most
issues can be discussed in 30 minutes.</p>
<p>When this happens, make sure that someone documents what is discussed in the
CL, so that the history is preserved.</p>
<h3 id="if-my-api-needs-to-violate-a-standard">...if my API needs to violate a standard?</h3>
<p>Clearly document (using an internal comment in the proto) that you are
violating an API design guideline and your rationale for doing so. This comment
<strong>must</strong> be prefixed with <code>aip.dev/not-precedent</code>.</p>
<p>In general, your rationale for the design guideline violation <strong>should</strong> be in
accordance with one of the enumerated reasons listed in <a href="/200">AIP-200</a>. If it is
not, work together with your API reviewer to determine the right thing to do.</p>
<h3 id="if-a-reviewer-is-bringing-up-a-previously-settled-issue">...if a reviewer is bringing up a previously-settled issue?</h3>
<p>If you have a different reviewer from your API's previous stages, this might
happen. In general, the best approach is simply to reference the code review
where the issue was decided. Reviewers want to avoid causing you churn, and
therefore usually give deference to previous reviews. This is usually
sufficient to resolve the question promptly.</p>
<p>Occasionally, the reviewer may believe that the previous reviewer made a
significant mistake, and that correcting it is important. In this case, you and
your reviewer should work together to determine the best course of action.</p>
<h3 id="if-the-team-and-the-reviewers-strongly-disagree">...if the team and the reviewers strongly disagree?</h3>
<p>Escalate according to <a href="/1">AIP-1</a>.</p>
<h2 id="does-my-pa-or-team-have-any-particular-guidelines">Does my PA or team have any particular guidelines?</h2>
<p>The Cloud PA has specific guidelines to ensure additional uniformity across
Cloud, and Cloud APIs have their own reviewer pool. Other teams may adopt
similar (but not necessarily identical) rules and systems. Some teams that
produce multiple APIs (for example, machine learning) may also have guidelines
that apply to that group of APIs.</p>
<p>In all cases, we endeavor to make these guidelines available as AIPs; the
higher AIP numbers are reserved for specific PA and team use (see <a href="/2">AIP-2</a>),
and these AIPs are listed in the <a href="/">AIP index</a>.</p>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-111</h4>
  <h1 id="planes">Planes</h1>
<p>Resources and methods on an API can be divided into the <em>plane</em> that they reside
or perform operations upon. For the context of APIs, the following planes are
defined:</p>
<ul>
<li>Management plane: a uniform, resource-oriented API that primarily
  configures and allows retrieval of resources.</li>
<li>Data plane: a heterogenous API (ideally resource-oriented) that reads and
  write user data. Often connects to entities provisioned by the management
  plane, such as virtual machines.</li>
</ul>
<p>The term "plane" was originally used in networking architecture. Although system
and network architecture often defines additional planes (e.g. control plane or
power planes), as the AIPs are focused on the interface, they are not defined in
this AIP.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<h3 id="management-plane">Management Plane</h3>
<p>Management resources and methods exist primarily to provision, configure, and
audit the resources that the data plane interfaces with.</p>
<p>As an example, the following are considered management resources for a cloud
provider:</p>
<ul>
<li>virtual machines</li>
<li>virtual private networks</li>
<li>virtual disks</li>
<li>a blob store instance</li>
<li>a project or account</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="data-plane">Data Plane</h3>
<p>Methods on the data plane operate on user data in a variety of data formats, and
generally interface with a resource provisioned via a management plane API.
Examples of data plane methods include:</p>
<ul>
<li>writing and reading rows in a table</li>
<li>pushing to or pulling from a message queue</li>
<li>uploading blobs to or downloading blobs from a blob store instance</li>
</ul>
<p>Data plane APIs <strong>may</strong> be heterogenous across a larger API surface, due to
requirements including high throughput, low latency, or the need to adhere to an
existing interface specification (e.g. ANSI SQL).</p>
<ul>
<li>For convenience, resources and methods that operate on the data plane <strong>may</strong>
expose themselves via resource-oriented management APIs. If so, those resources
and methods <strong>must</strong> adhere to the requirements of the management plane as
specified in the other AIPs (<a href="/131">AIP-131</a> through <a href="/135">AIP-135</a>).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="major-distinctions-between-management-and-data-plane">Major distinctions between management and data plane</h3>
<ul>
<li><a href="/9#declarative-clients">Declarative clients</a> operate on the management plane exclusively.</li>
<li>Data planes are often on the critical path of user-facing functionality, and
  therefore:<ul>
<li>Have higher availability requirements than management planes.</li>
<li>Are more performance-sensitive than management planes.</li>
<li>Require higher-throughput than management planes.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2023-06-10</strong>: Introduction of this AIP.</li>
</ul>
