  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-135</h4>
  <h1 id="standard-methods-delete">Standard methods: Delete</h1>
<p>In REST APIs, it is customary to make a <code>DELETE</code> request to a resource's URI
(for example, <code>/v1/publishers/{publisher}/books/{book}</code>) in order to delete
that resource.</p>
<p>Resource-oriented design (<a href="/121">AIP-121</a>) honors this pattern through the <code>Delete</code>
method. These RPCs accept the URI representing that resource and usually return
an empty response.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>APIs <strong>should</strong> generally provide a delete method for resources unless it is
not valuable for users to do so.</p>
<p>Delete methods are specified using the following pattern:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">DeleteBook</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">DeleteBookRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.protobuf.Empty</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">delete</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{name=publishers/*/books/*}&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.method_signature</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;name&quot;</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>The RPC's name <strong>must</strong> begin with the word <code>Delete</code>. The remainder of the
  RPC name <strong>should</strong> be the singular form of the resource's message name.</li>
<li>The request message <strong>must</strong> match the RPC name, with a <code>Request</code> suffix.</li>
<li>The response message <strong>should</strong> be <code>google.protobuf.Empty</code>.<ul>
<li>If the resource is <a href="#soft-delete">soft deleted</a>, the response message
  <strong>should</strong> be the resource itself.</li>
<li>If the delete RPC is <a href="#long-running-delete">long-running</a>, the response
  message <strong>must</strong> be a <code>google.longrunning.Operation</code> which resolves to the
  correct response.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The HTTP verb <strong>must</strong> be <code>DELETE</code>.</li>
<li>The request message field receiving the resource name <strong>should</strong> map to the
  URI path.<ul>
<li>This field <strong>should</strong> be called <code>name</code>.</li>
<li>The <code>name</code> field <strong>should</strong> be the only variable in the URI path. All
  remaining parameters <strong>should</strong> map to URI query parameters.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>There <strong>must not</strong> be a <code>body</code> key in the <code>google.api.http</code> annotation.</li>
<li>There <strong>should</strong> be exactly one <code>google.api.method_signature</code> annotation,
  with a value of <code>"name"</code>. If an etag or force field are used, they <strong>may</strong> be
  included in the signature.</li>
<li>If the API is operating on the <a href="/111#management-plane">Management Plane</a>, the operation should have
  <a href="/121#strong-consistency">strong consistency</a>: the completion of a delete operation <strong>must</strong> mean
  that the existence of the resource has reached a steady-state and reading
  resource state returns a consistent response.</li>
<li>The API <strong>must</strong> fail with a <code>FAILED_PRECONDITION</code> error if child resources
  are present. See guidance on <a href="#cascading-delete">Cascading Delete</a> if forcing
  deletion of parent and child resources is necessary.<ul>
<li>If the only child resource type is a <a href="/156">Singleton</a>, deletion <strong>must</strong>
  be allowed, because the lifecycle of a Singleton is tied to that of its
  parent resource. This applies even if there are multiple different Singleton
  resource types for the same parent resource.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>The Delete method <strong>should</strong> succeed if and only if a resource was present and
was successfully deleted. If the resource did not exist, the method <strong>should</strong>
send a <code>NOT_FOUND</code> error.</p>
<h3 id="request-message">Request message</h3>
<p>Delete methods implement a common request message pattern:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">DeleteBookRequest</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The name of the book to delete.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Format: publishers/{publisher}/books/{book}</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">name</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.field_behavior</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">REQUIRED</span><span class="p">,</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.resource_reference</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">      </span><span class="n">type</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;library.googleapis.com/Book&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">}];</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>A <code>name</code> field <strong>must</strong> be included. It <strong>should</strong> be called <code>name</code>.<ul>
<li>The field <strong>should</strong> be <a href="/203">annotated as required</a>.</li>
<li>The field <strong>must</strong> identify the <a href="/123">resource type</a> that it
  references.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The comment for the field <strong>should</strong> document the resource pattern.</li>
<li>The request message <strong>must not</strong> contain any other required fields, and
  <strong>should not</strong> contain other optional fields except those described in this
  or another AIP.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="soft-delete">Soft delete</h3>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> This material was moved into its own document to provide a more
comprehensive treatment: <a href="/164">AIP-164</a>.</p>
<h3 id="long-running-delete">Long-running delete</h3>
<p>Some resources take longer to delete a resource than is reasonable for a
regular API request. In this situation, the API <strong>should</strong> use a long-running
operation instead:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">DeleteBook</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">DeleteBookRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.longrunning.Operation</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">delete</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{name=publishers/*/books/*}&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.longrunning.operation_info</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">response_type</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;google.protobuf.Empty&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">metadata_type</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;OperationMetadata&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>The response type <strong>must</strong> be set to the appropriate return type if the RPC
  was not long-running: <code>google.protobuf.Empty</code> for most Delete RPCs, or the
  resource itself for soft delete (<a href="/164">AIP-164</a>).</li>
<li>Both the <code>response_type</code> and <code>metadata_type</code> fields <strong>must</strong> be specified
  (even if they are <code>google.protobuf.Empty</code>).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="cascading-delete">Cascading delete</h3>
<p>Sometimes, it may be necessary for users to be able to delete a resource as
well as all applicable child resources. However, since deletion is usually
permanent, it is also important that users not do so accidentally, as
reconstructing wiped-out child resources may be quite difficult.</p>
<p>If an API allows deletion of a resource that may have child resources, the API
<strong>should</strong> provide a <code>bool force</code> field on the request, which the user sets to
explicitly opt in to a cascading delete.</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">DeletePublisherRequest</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The name of the publisher to delete.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Format: publishers/{publisher}</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">name</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.field_behavior</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">REQUIRED</span><span class="p">,</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.resource_reference</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">      </span><span class="n">type</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;library.googleapis.com/Publisher&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">}];</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// If set to true, any books from this publisher will also be deleted.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// (Otherwise, the request will only work if the publisher has no books.)</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">bool</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">force</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>The API <strong>must</strong> fail with a <code>FAILED_PRECONDITION</code> error if the <code>force</code> field
is <code>false</code> (or unset) and child resources are present.</p>
<h3 id="protected-delete">Protected delete</h3>
<p>Sometimes, it may be necessary for users to ensure that no changes have been
made to a resource that is being deleted. If a resource provides an <a href="/134#etags">etag</a>,
the delete request <strong>may</strong> accept the etag (as either required or optional):</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">DeleteBookRequest</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The name of the book to delete.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Format: publishers/{publisher}/books/{book}</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">name</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.field_behavior</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">REQUIRED</span><span class="p">,</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.resource_reference</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">      </span><span class="n">type</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;library.googleapis.com/Book&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">}];</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Optional. The etag of the book.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// If this is provided, it must match the server&#39;s etag.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">etag</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>If the etag is provided and does not match the server-computed etag, the
request <strong>must</strong> fail with a <code>ABORTED</code> error code.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Declarative-friendly resources (<a href="/128">AIP-128</a>) <strong>must</strong> provide the <code>etag</code>
field for Delete requests.</p>
<h3 id="delete-if-existing">Delete if existing</h3>
<p>If the service uses client-assigned resource names, <code>Delete</code> methods <strong>may</strong>
expose a <code>bool allow_missing</code> field, which will cause the method to succeed in
the event that the user attempts to delete a resource that is not present (in
which case the request is a no-op):</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">DeleteBookRequest</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The book to delete.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Format: publishers/{publisher}/books/{book}</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">name</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.field_behavior</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">REQUIRED</span><span class="p">,</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.resource_reference</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">type</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;library.googleapis.com/Book&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">];</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// If set to true, and the book is not found, the request will succeed</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// but no action will be taken on the server</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">bool</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">allow_missing</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>More specifically, the <code>allow_missing</code> flag triggers the following behavior:</p>
<ul>
<li>If the method call is on a resource that does not exist, the request is a
  no-op.<ul>
<li>The <code>etag</code> field is ignored.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>If the method call is on a resource that already exists, the resource is
  deleted (subject to other checks).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Declarative-friendly resources (<a href="/128">AIP-128</a>) <strong>should</strong> expose the
<code>bool allow_missing</code> field.</p>
<h3 id="errors">Errors</h3>
<p>If the user does not have permission to access the resource, regardless of
whether or not it exists, the service <strong>must</strong> error with <code>PERMISSION_DENIED</code>
(HTTP 403). Permission <strong>must</strong> be checked prior to checking if the resource
exists.</p>
<p>If the user does have proper permission, but the requested resource does not
exist, the service <strong>must</strong> error with <code>NOT_FOUND</code> (HTTP 404) unless
<code>allow_missing</code> is set to <code>true</code>.</p>
<h2 id="further-reading">Further reading</h2>
<ul>
<li>For soft delete and undelete, see <a href="/164">AIP-164</a>.</li>
<li>For bulk deleting large numbers of resources based on a filter, see <a href="/165">AIP-165</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2024-06-11</strong>: Add deletion behavior for parent resource deletion requests without a <code>force</code> field.</li>
<li><strong>2023-08-24</strong>: Adding consistency requirement.</li>
<li><strong>2022-06-02:</strong> Changed suffix descriptions to eliminate superfluous "-".</li>
<li><strong>2022-02-02</strong>: Changed eTag error from <code>FAILED_PRECONDITION</code> to <code>ABORTED</code> making it consistent with change to <a href="/154">AIP-154</a> &amp; <a href="/134#etags">AIP-134</a> on 2021-03-05.</li>
<li><strong>2020-10-06</strong>: Added guidance for declarative-friendly resources.</li>
<li><strong>2020-10-06</strong>: Added guidance for allowing no-op delete for missing
  resources.</li>
<li><strong>2020-10-06</strong>: Moved soft delete and undelete guidance into a new <a href="/164">AIP-164</a>.</li>
<li><strong>2020-06-08</strong>: Added guidance for <code>Get</code> of soft-deleted resources.</li>
<li><strong>2020-02-03</strong>: Added guidance for error cases.</li>
<li><strong>2019-10-18</strong>: Added guidance on annotations.</li>
<li><strong>2019-08-01</strong>: Changed the examples from "shelves" to "publishers", to
  present a better example of resource ownership.</li>
<li><strong>2019-06-10</strong>: Added guidance for long-running delete.</li>
<li><strong>2019-05-29</strong>: Added an explicit prohibition on arbitrary fields in standard
  methods.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-136</h4>
  <h1 id="custom-methods">Custom methods</h1>
<p>Resource-oriented design (<a href="/121">AIP-121</a>) uses custom methods to provide a means to
express arbitrary actions that are difficult to model using only the standard
methods. Custom methods are important because they provide a means for an API's
vocabulary to adhere to user intent.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>Custom methods <strong>should</strong> only be used for functionality that can not be easily
expressed via standard methods; prefer standard methods if possible, due to
their consistent semantics. (Of course, this only applies if the functionality
in question actually conforms to the normal semantics; it is <em>not</em> a good idea
to contort things to endeavor to make the standard methods "sort of work".)</p>
<p>While custom methods vary widely in how they are designed, many principles
apply consistently:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// Archives the given book.</span>
<span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">ArchiveBook</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ArchiveBookRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ArchiveBookResponse</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">post</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{name=publishers/*/books/*}:archive&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">body</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;*&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> The pattern above shows a custom method that operates on a specific
resource. Custom methods can be associated with resources, collections, or
services. The bullets below apply in all three cases.</p>
<ul>
<li>The name of the method <strong>should</strong> be a verb followed by a noun.<ul>
<li>The name <strong>must not</strong> contain prepositions ("for", "with", etc.).</li>
<li>The verb in the name <strong>should not</strong> contain any of the standard method verbs (<a href="/131">Get</a>,
  <a href="/132">List</a>, <a href="/133">Create</a>, <a href="/134">Update</a>, <a href="/135">Delete</a>).</li>
<li>The name <strong>must not</strong> include the term <code>Async</code>. Instead, if the intention is
  to differentiate between immediate and long-running RPCs, the suffix <code>LongRunning</code>
  <strong>may</strong> be used for this purpose. For example, to create a long-running book creation
  RPC (if the standard <code>CreateBook</code> method was designed before long-running aspects were
  considered), a custom <code>CreateBookLongRunning</code> method could be introduced.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The HTTP method <strong>must</strong> be <code>GET</code> or <code>POST</code>:<ul>
<li><code>GET</code> <strong>must</strong> be used for methods retrieving data or resource state.<ul>
<li><code>POST</code> <strong>may</strong> be used for data retrieval methods if the request payload could
  exceed URL size limitations, thus requiring a <code>body</code>.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><code>POST</code> <strong>must</strong> be used if the method has side effects or mutates resources
  or data.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The HTTP URI <strong>must</strong> use a <code>:</code> character followed by the custom verb
  (<code>:archive</code> in the above example), and the verb in the URI <strong>must</strong> match the
  verb in the name of the RPC.<ul>
<li>If word separation is required, <code>camelCase</code> <strong>must</strong> be used.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The <code>body</code> clause in the <code>google.api.http</code> annotation <strong>should</strong> be <code>"*"</code>.<ul>
<li>See <a href="/127">HTTP and gRPC Transcoding</a> for more information.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Custom methods <strong>should</strong> take a request message matching the RPC
  name, with a <code>Request</code> suffix.</li>
<li>Custom methods <strong>should</strong> return a response message matching the RPC
  name, with a <code>Response</code> suffix.<ul>
<li>When operating on a specific resource, a custom method <strong>may</strong> return the
  resource itself.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="resource-based-custom-methods">Resource-based custom methods</h3>
<p>Custom methods <strong>must</strong> operate on a resource if the API can be modeled
as such:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// Archives the given book.</span>
<span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">ArchiveBook</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ArchiveBookRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ArchiveBookResponse</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">post</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{name=publishers/*/books/*}:archive&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">body</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;*&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>The parameter for the resource's name <strong>must</strong> be called <code>name</code>, and
  be the only variable in the URI path.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="collection-based-custom-methods">Collection-based custom methods</h3>
<p>While most custom methods operate on a single resource, some custom methods
<strong>may</strong> operate on a collection instead:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// Sorts the books from this publisher.</span>
<span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">SortBooks</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">SortBooksRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">SortBooksResponse</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">post</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{parent=publishers/*}/books:sort&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">body</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;*&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>If the collection's resource has a parent, that resource <strong>must</strong> be called
  <code>parent</code> and be the only variable in the URI path.</li>
<li>The collection key (<code>books</code> in the above example) <strong>must</strong> be literal.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="stateless-methods">Stateless methods</h3>
<p>Some custom methods are not attached to resources at all. These methods are
generally <em>stateless</em>: they accept a request and return a response, and have no
permanent effect on data within the API.</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// Translates the provided text from one language to another.</span>
<span class="k">rpc</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">TranslateText</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">TranslateTextRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="k">returns</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">TranslateTextResponse</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="k">option</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">google.api.http</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">post</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;/v1/{project=projects/*}:translateText&quot;</span>
<span class="w">    </span><span class="n">body</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s">&quot;*&quot;</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="p">};</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>If the method runs in a particular scope (such as a project, as in the above
  example), the field name in the request message <strong>should</strong> be the name of the
  scope resource. If word separators are necessary, <code>snake_case</code> <strong>must</strong> be
  used.</li>
<li>The URI <strong>should</strong> place both the verb and noun after the <code>:</code> separator
  (avoid a "faux collection key" in the URI in this case, as there is no
  collection). For example, <code>:translateText</code> is preferable to <code>text:translate</code>.</li>
<li>Stateless methods <strong>must</strong> use <code>POST</code> if they involve billing.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="declarative-friendly-resources">Declarative-friendly resources</h3>
<p>Declarative-friendly resources usually <strong>should not</strong> employ custom methods
(except specific declarative-friendly custom methods discussed in other AIPs),
because declarative-friendly tools are unable to automatically determine what
to do with them.</p>
<p>An exception to this is for rarely-used, fundamentally imperative operations,
such as a <code>Move</code> or <code>Rename</code> operation, for which there would not be an
expectation of declarative support.</p>
<h2 id="rationale">Rationale</h2>
<h3 id="http-path">HTTP path</h3>
<p>Similar to standard methods, a custom method that operates on a resource or
collection needs a <code>name</code> or <code>parent</code> parameter to indicate the resource that it
operates on. This convention allows clients to map custom methods to the
appropriate resource.</p>
<h3 id="http-methods">HTTP methods</h3>
<p>Allowing both <code>GET</code> and <code>POST</code> HTTP verbs allows a clear distinction for
which methods do not mutate data, and which ones do. Methods that only
read data have first-class concepts in some clients (DataSources in
Terraform) and clearly indicate to a user which methods can be called
without risk of runtime impact.</p>
<p>Allowing <code>POST</code> to be used for requests which would otherwise be made using
<code>GET</code> is a convenience:</p>
<ul>
<li>It avoids large query strings leading to requests which violate URL size
  limitations.</li>
<li>It allows clients to implement a single way of serializing request data, or
  at least avoids them from having to implement complex rules for repeated
  fields etc.</li>
<li>It allows RPCs which might normally be simple to still contain data for
  complex situations where that data may not be representable via query
  parameters.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="disallowing-prepositions">Disallowing prepositions</h3>
<p>Generally, method names with prepositions indicate that a new method is being
used where a field should instead be added to an existing method, or the method
should use a distinct verb. For example, if a <code>CreateBook</code> message already
exists and you are considering adding <code>CreateBookFromDictation</code>, consider a
<code>TranscribeBook</code> method instead. Similarly, if there is desire for a
property-specific look-up method, instead of <code>GetBookByAuthor</code> consider a
<code>SearchBooks</code> with an <code>author</code> field as a search dimension. This helps prevent
an explosion of hyper-focused methods that bloat API and client surfaces, and
add complexity to both managing and consuming the API.</p>
<h3 id="rpc-name">RPC name</h3>
<p>The term "async" is commonly used in programming languages to indicate whether
a specific method call is synchronous or asynchronous, including for making RPCs.
That sync/async aspect is at a different abstraction level to whether the RPC
itself is intended to start a long-running operation. Using "async" within the
RPC name itself causes confusion, and can even cause issues for client libraries
which generate both synchronous and asynchronous methods to call the RPC in some
languages.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2026-06-09:</strong> Allow complex GET to be POST if necessary.</li>
<li><strong>2025-05-12:</strong> Extend disallowing prepositions rationale.</li>
<li><strong>2025-01-09:</strong> Add original rationale for disallowing prepositions in names.</li>
<li><strong>2023-11-16:</strong> Included link to <a href="/127">AIP-127</a> "HTTP and gRPC Transcoding" for guidance on body definition.</li>
<li><strong>2023-05-16:</strong> Added prohibition of the term "async" within RPC names.</li>
<li><strong>2023-05-09:</strong> Adding guidance for POST and GET, require parent instead of
  the resource singular.</li>
<li><strong>2023-03-02:</strong> Explicitly discourage use of standard method verbs.</li>
<li><strong>2022-06-02:</strong> Changed suffix descriptions to eliminate superfluous "-".</li>
<li><strong>2020-10-06:</strong> Added declarative-friendly guidance.</li>
<li><strong>2019-08-01:</strong> Changed the examples from "shelves" to "publishers", to
  present a better example of resource ownership.</li>
</ul>

</li>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-140</h4>
  <h1 id="field-names">Field names</h1>
<p>Naming fields in a way that is intuitive to users can often be one of the most
challenging aspects of designing an API. This is true for many reasons; often a
field name that seems entirely intuitive to the author can baffle a reader.</p>
<p>Additionally, users rarely use only one API; they use many APIs together. As a
result, a single company using the same name to mean different things (or
different names to mean the same thing) can often cause unnecessary confusion,
because users can no longer take what they've already learned from one API and
apply that to another.</p>
<p>In short, APIs are easiest to understand when field names are simple,
intuitive, and consistent with one another.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>Field names <strong>should</strong> be in correct American English.</p>
<p>Field names <strong>should</strong> clearly and precisely communicate the concept being
presented and avoid overly general names that are ambiguous. That said, field
names <strong>should</strong> avoid including unnecessary words. In particular, avoid
including adjectives that always apply and add little cognitive value. For
example, a <code>proxy_settings</code> field might be as helpful as
<code>shared_proxy_settings</code> if there is no unshared variant.</p>
<p><strong>Important:</strong> Field names often appear in generated client surfaces. Ensure they 
are appropriately descriptive and of suitable length.</p>
<h3 id="case">Case</h3>
<p>Field definitions in protobuf files <strong>must</strong> use <code>lower_snake_case</code> names.
These names are mapped to an appropriate naming convention in JSON and in
generated code.</p>
<p>Additionally, each word in the field <strong>must not</strong> begin with a number, because
it creates ambiguity when converting between snake case and camel case.
Similarly, fields <strong>must not</strong> contain leading, trailing, or adjacent
underscores.</p>
<h3 id="uniformity">Uniformity</h3>
<p>APIs <strong>should</strong> endeavor to use the same name for the same concept and
different names for different concepts wherever possible. This includes names
across multiple APIs, in particular if those APIs are likely to be used
together.</p>
<h3 id="repeated-fields">Repeated fields</h3>
<p>Repeated fields <strong>must</strong> use the proper plural form, such as <code>books</code> or
<code>authors</code>. On the other hand, non-repeated fields <strong>should</strong> use the singular
form such as <code>book</code> or <code>author</code>. This implies that resource names <strong>should</strong>
use the singular form as well, since the field name should follow the resource
name (e.g., use <code>repeated Book books</code>, <strong>not</strong> <code>Books books = 1</code>).</p>
<h3 id="prepositions">Prepositions</h3>
<p>Field names <strong>should not</strong> include prepositions (such as "with", "for", "at",
"by", etc). For example:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>error_reason</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>reason_for_error</code>)</li>
<li><code>author</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>written_by</code>)</li>
</ul>
<p>It is easier for field names to match more often when following this
convention. Additionally, prepositions in field names may also indicate a
design concern, such as an overly-restrictive field or a sub-optimal data type.
This is particularly true regarding "with": a field named <code>book_with_publisher</code>
likely indicates that the book resource may be improperly structured and worth
redesigning.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> The word "per" is an exception to this rule. See <a href="/141">AIP-141</a> for 
guidance in the case where "per" is used as part of a unit (e.g. "miles per hour").</p>
<h3 id="abbreviations">Abbreviations</h3>
<p>For well known name abbreviations among software developers, such as "config"
and "spec", the abbreviations <strong>should</strong> be used in API definitions instead of
the full spelling. This will make the source code easy to read and write.
Examples:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>config</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>configuration</code>)</li>
<li><code>id</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>identifier</code>)</li>
<li><code>info</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>information</code>)</li>
<li><code>spec</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>specification</code>)</li>
<li><code>stats</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>statistics</code>)</li>
</ul>
<p>Furthermore, well known abbreviations for units <strong>should</strong> be used in field names.
See <a href="/141">AIP-141</a> for more guidance on fields that represent quantities. Examples:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>distance_km</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>distance_kilometers</code>)</li>
<li><code>width_px</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>width_pixels</code>)</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="adjectives">Adjectives</h3>
<p>For uniformity, field names that contain both a noun and an adjective
<strong>should</strong> place the adjective <em>before</em> the noun. For example:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>collected_items</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>items_collected</code>)</li>
<li><code>imported_objects</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>objects_imported</code>)</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="verbs">Verbs</h3>
<p>Field names <strong>must not</strong> be named to reflect an intent or action. They
<strong>must not</strong> be verbs. Rather, because the field defines the <em>desired
value</em> for mutations, e.g. Create and Update, and the <em>current value</em>
for reads, e.g.  Get and List, the name <strong>must</strong> be a noun. It defines
what is so, not what to do.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>collected_items</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>collect_items</code>)</li>
<li><code>disabled</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>disable</code>)</li>
</ul>
<p>In contrast, method names, whether standard or custom, change facets of
resources and are named as verbs.</p>
<h3 id="booleans">Booleans</h3>
<p>Boolean fields <strong>should</strong> omit the prefix "is". For example:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>disabled</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>is_disabled</code>)</li>
<li><code>required</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>is_required</code>)</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Field names that would otherwise be <a href="#reserved-words">reserved words</a>
are an exception to this rule. For example, <code>is_new</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>new</code>).</p>
<h3 id="string-vs-bytes">String vs. bytes</h3>
<p>When using <code>bytes</code>, the contents of the field are base64-encoded when using
JSON on the wire. Services <strong>should</strong> use <code>bytes</code> when there is a need to send
binary contents over the wire, and <strong>should not</strong> ask the user to manually
base64-encode a field into a <code>string</code> field. The one exception is when the
API is designed to handle data that is meant to be base64-encoded at rest and
the double base64-encoding as a result of using <code>bytes</code> is undesirable - in
this case, services <strong>may</strong> use a <code>string</code>.</p>
<h3 id="uris">URIs</h3>
<p>Field names representing arbitrary URIs <strong>should</strong> use <code>uri</code>. In particular,
note that URLs are URIs but not all URIs are URLs.</p>
<p>Field names <strong>may</strong> use a prefix in front of <code>uri</code> as appropriate.</p>
<p>Field names that can only represent a URL <strong>should</strong> use <code>url</code>.</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">Book</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">name</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[(</span><span class="n">google.api.field_behavior</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="n">IDENTIFIER</span><span class="p">];</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// A URL pointing to an image of the book.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">image_url</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// A URI identifying the book.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// This could be an ISBN or a URL.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">uri</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> APIs that have previously used <code>uri</code> for URL fields may continue to
do so to avoid unnecessary API changes and to preserve local consistency.</p>
<h3 id="reserved-words">Reserved words</h3>
<p>Field names <strong>should</strong> avoid using names that are likely to conflict with
keywords in common programming languages, such as <code>new</code>, <code>class</code>, <code>function</code>,
<code>import</code>, etc. Reserved keywords can cause hardship for developers using the
API in that language.</p>
<h3 id="conflicts">Conflicts</h3>
<p>Messages <strong>should not</strong> include a field with the same name as the enclosing
message (ignoring case transformations). This causes conflicts when generating
code in some languages.</p>
<h3 id="display-names">Display names</h3>
<p>Many resources have a human-readable name, often used for display in UI. This
field <strong>should</strong> be called <code>display_name</code>, and <strong>should not</strong> have a uniqueness
requirement.</p>
<p>If an entity has an official, formal name (such as a company name or the title
of a book), an API <strong>may</strong> use <code>title</code> as the field name instead. The <code>title</code>
field <strong>should not</strong> have a uniqueness requirement.</p>
<h2 id="further-reading">Further reading</h2>
<ul>
<li>For naming resource fields, see <a href="/122">AIP-122</a>.</li>
<li>For naming fields representing quantities, see <a href="/141">AIP-141</a>.</li>
<li>For naming fields representing time, see <a href="/142">AIP-142</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="rationale">Rationale</h2>
<h3 id="uri-vs-url">URI vs URL</h3>
<p>The guidance itself mentions that all URLs are URIs, but not all URIs are URLs.
The goal of aligning on URI is to enable a more generalizable field, that can
handle a variety of use cases, as well as drive standardization across APIs,
creating a more coherent surface. At the same time, the requirement being a
<strong>should</strong> allows for more specific terms when it truly merits it.</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>2025-10-23</strong>: Call out <a href="/141">AIP-141</a> unit abbreviations as preferred.</li>
<li><strong>2025-03-10</strong>: Add rationale for URI guidance.</li>
<li><strong>2024-12-20</strong>: Copy over abbreviations guidance from old design site.</li>
<li><strong>2024-08-26</strong>: Codify exception to string and base64 guidance </li>
<li><strong>2024-05-18</strong>: Documented the effect of field names on client surfaces.</li>
<li><strong>2023-04-25</strong>: Field names <strong>must not</strong> be expressed as verbs.</li>
<li><strong>2021-07-12</strong>: Normalized display name guidance to "should".</li>
<li><strong>2021-04-07</strong>: Added base64 and bytes guidance.</li>
<li><strong>2021-03-05</strong>: Added prohibition on leading, trailing, or adjacent
  underscores.</li>
<li><strong>2020-06-10</strong>: Added prohibition on starting any word with a number.</li>
<li><strong>2020-05-29</strong>: Added guidance around URIs.</li>
<li><strong>2020-03-24</strong>: Added guidance around conflicting field and message names.</li>
<li><strong>2020-01-30</strong>: Added guidance around <code>display_name</code> and <code>title</code>.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-141</h4>
  <h1 id="quantities">Quantities</h1>
<p>Many services need to represent a discrete quantity of items (number of bytes,
number of miles, number of nodes, etc.).</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>Quantities with a clear unit of measurement (such as bytes, miles, and so on)
<strong>must</strong> include the unit of measurement as the suffix. When appropriate, units
<strong>should</strong> use generally accepted abbreviations, and abbreviations <strong>should not</strong> 
be pluralized (for example, <code>distance_km</code> rather than <code>distance_kilometers</code>). </p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// A representation of a non-stop air route.</span>
<span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">Route</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The airport where the route begins.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">origin</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The destination airport.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">destination</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The distance between the origin and destination airports.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// This value is also used to determine the credited frequent flyer miles.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">int32</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">distance_miles</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p>If the quantity is a number of items (for example, the number of nodes in a
cluster), then the field <strong>should</strong> use the suffix <code>_count</code> (<strong>not</strong> the prefix
<code>num_</code>):</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// A cluster of individual nodes.</span>
<span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">Cluster</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The number of nodes in the cluster.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">int32</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">node_count</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Fields <strong>must not</strong> use unsigned integer types, because many
programming languages and systems do not support them well.</p>
<h3 id="compound-units">Compound units</h3>
<p>Quantities with compound units of measurement <strong>may</strong> use separating underscores
between units as needed for clarity. Unabbreviated units <strong>must</strong> be separated.
Abbreviated units <strong>should not</strong> be separated unless otherwise ambiguous.
Compound units <strong>should</strong> be in plural form, with all component units in 
singular form except for the final component unit, which should be in plural 
form unless abbreviated.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>energy_kwh</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>energy_kw_h</code>)</li>
<li><code>energy_kw_fortnights</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>energy_kwfortnight</code> or <code>energy_kw_fortnight</code>)</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Metric prefixes <strong>must not</strong> be separated from their base unit.</p>
<h3 id="inverse-units">Inverse units</h3>
<p>Quantities with units of measurement that are or include inverse units
<strong>should</strong> indicate all inverse units as a compound unit after a compound
of any non-inverse units, separated by the word "per".
The inverse compound unit <strong>should</strong> be in singular form.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>speed_miles_per_hour</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>speed_mph</code>)</li>
<li><code>speed_meters_per_second</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>speed_meters_per_seconds</code> or <code>speed_meter_per_second</code>)</li>
<li><code>event_count_per_hour</code> (<strong>not</strong> <code>events_per_hour</code>, <code>event_counts_per_hour</code>, or <code>hourly_events</code>)</li>
<li><code>price_per_kwh</code> (using <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto"><code>google.type.Money</code></a>)</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> This guidance does not apply in cases where generally accepted derived
units with special names and symbols exist for inverse quantities. For example,
the derived unit 'hertz' <strong>should</strong> be used when appropriate for reciprocal time.</p>
<h3 id="specialized-messages">Specialized messages</h3>
<p>It is sometimes useful to create a message that represents a particular
quantity. This is particularly valuable in two situations:</p>
<ul>
<li>Grouping two or more individual quantities together. Example:
  <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/duration.proto"><code>google.protobuf.Duration</code></a></li>
<li>Representing a common concept where the unit of measurement may itself vary.
  Example: <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto"><code>google.type.Money</code></a></li>
</ul>
<p>APIs <strong>may</strong> create messages to represent quantities when appropriate. When
using these messages as fields, APIs <strong>should</strong> use the name of the message as
the suffix for the field name if it makes intuitive sense to do so.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2025-07-09</strong>: Added guidance for compound units.</li>
<li><strong>2025-07-09</strong>: Clarified guidance to not pluralize abbreviated units.</li>
<li><strong>2025-07-09</strong>: Clarified guidance to use per_ prefix to represent inverse units.</li>
<li><strong>2019-09-13</strong>: Added the prohibition on uint and fixed types.</li>
</ul>

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-142</h4>
  <h1 id="time-and-duration">Time and duration</h1>
<p>Many services need to represent the concepts surrounding time. Representing
time can be challenging due to the intricacies of calendars and time zones, as
well as the fact that common exchange formats (such as JSON) lack a native
concept of time.</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>Fields representing time <strong>should</strong> use the common, generally used components
(such as <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto"><code>google.protobuf.Timestamp</code></a> or
<a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/date.proto"><code>google.type.Date</code></a>) for representing time or duration types. These
types are <a href="/213">common components</a>, and using them consistently allows
infrastructure and tooling to provide a better experience when interacting with
time values.</p>
<h3 id="timestamps">Timestamps</h3>
<p>Fields that represent an absolute point in time (independent of any time zone
or calendar) <strong>should</strong> use the <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto"><code>google.protobuf.Timestamp</code></a> type,
(which uses UNIX timestamps under the hood and hold nanosecond precision).</p>
<p>These fields <strong>should</strong> have names ending in <code>_time</code>, such as <code>create_time</code> or
<code>update_time</code>. For repeated fields, the names <strong>should</strong> end in <code>_times</code>
instead.</p>
<p>Many timestamp fields refer to an activity (for example, <code>create_time</code> refers
to when the applicable resource was created). For these, the field <strong>should</strong>
be named with the <code>{imperative}_time</code> form. For example, if a book is being
published, the field storing the time when this happens would use the
imperative form of the verb "to publish" ("publish") resulting in a field
called <code>publish_time</code>. Fields <strong>should not</strong> be named using the past tense
(such as <code>published_time</code>, <code>created_time</code> or <code>last_updated_time</code>).</p>
<h3 id="durations">Durations</h3>
<p>Fields that represent a span between two points in time (independent of any
time zone or calendar) <strong>should</strong> use the
<a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/duration.proto"><code>google.protobuf.Duration</code></a> type.</p>
<p>To illustrate the distinction between timestamps and durations, consider a
flight record:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// A representation of a (very incomplete) flight log.</span>
<span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">FlightRecord</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The absolute point in time when the plane took off.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="n">google.protobuf.Timestamp</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">takeoff_time</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The length (duration) of the flight, from takeoff to landing.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="n">google.protobuf.Duration</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">flight_duration</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Observant readers may notice that the <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto">timestamp</a> and <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/duration.proto">duration</a>
messages have the same structure (<code>int64 seconds</code> and <code>int32 nanos</code>). However,
the distinction between these is important, because they have different
semantic meaning. Additionally, tooling is able to base behavior off of which
message is used. For example, a Python-based tool could convert timestamps to
<a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> objects and durations to <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.timedelta">timedelta</a>
objects.</p>
<h3 id="relative-time-segments">Relative time segments</h3>
<p>In some cases, it may be necessary to represent a time segment inside a stream.
In these cases, the <a href="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/duration.proto"><code>google.protobuf.Duration</code></a> type <strong>should</strong> be
used, and the field name <strong>should</strong> end with <code>_offset</code>. To ensure that the
meaning is clear, the field <strong>must</strong> have a comment noting the point that the
offset is relative to.</p>
<p>To illustrate this, consider a resource representing a segment of an audio
stream:</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">AudioSegment</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The duration relative to the start of the stream representing the</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// beginning of the segment.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="n">google.protobuf.Duration</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">start_offset</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The total length of the segment.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="n">google.protobuf.Duration</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">segment_duration</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<h3 id="civil-dates-and-times">Civil dates and times</h3>
<p>Fields that represent a calendar date or wall-clock time <strong>should</strong> use the
appropriate common components:</p>
<ul>
<li>Civil date: <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/date.proto"><code>google.type.Date</code></a></li>
<li>Wall-clock time: <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/timeofday.proto"><code>google.type.TimeOfDay</code></a></li>
</ul>
<p>Fields representing civil dates <strong>should</strong> have names ending in <code>_date</code>, while
fields representing civil times or datetimes <strong>should</strong> have names ending in
<code>_time</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Both the <code>Date</code> and <code>TimeOfDay</code> components are timezone-naïve. Fields
that require timezone-awareness <strong>should</strong> use <code>DateTime</code> (see below).</p>
<h3 id="civil-timestamps">Civil timestamps</h3>
<p>Fields that represent a civil timestamp (date and time, optionally with a time
zone) <strong>should</strong> use the <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/datetime.proto"><code>google.type.DateTime</code></a> component, and the
field name <strong>should</strong> end in <code>_time</code>.</p>
<h3 id="compatibility">Compatibility</h3>
<p>Occasionally, APIs are unable to use the common structures for legacy or
compatibility reasons. For example, an API may conform to a separate
specification that mandates that timestamps be integers or <a href="https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html">ISO-8601</a>
strings.</p>
<p>In these situations, fields <strong>may</strong> use other types. If possible, the following
naming conventions apply:</p>
<ul>
<li>For integers, include the meaning (examples: <code>time</code>, <code>duration</code>, <code>delay</code>,
  <code>latency</code>) <strong>and</strong> the unit of measurement (valid values: <code>seconds</code>,
  <code>millis</code>, <code>micros</code>, <code>nanos</code>) as a final suffix. For example,
  <code>send_time_millis</code>.</li>
<li>For strings, include the meaning (examples: <code>time</code>, <code>duration</code>, <code>delay</code>,
  <code>latency</code>) but no unit suffix.</li>
</ul>
<p>In all cases, clearly document the expected format, and the rationale for its
use.</p>
<!-- prettier-ignore-start -->

  <h4 class="aip-number">AIP-143</h4>
  <h1 id="standardized-codes">Standardized codes</h1>
<p>Many common concepts, such as spoken languages, countries, currency, and so on,
have common codes (usually formalized by the <a href="https://www.iso.org/">International Organization for
Standardization</a>) that are used in data communication and processing.
These codes address the issue that there are often different ways to express
the same concept in written language (for example, "United States" and "USA",
or "Español" and "Spanish").</p>
<h2 id="guidance">Guidance</h2>
<p>For concepts where a standardized code exists and is in common use, fields
representing these concepts <strong>should</strong> use the standardized code for both input
and output.</p>
<div class="highlight language-proto"><pre><span></span><code><span class="c1">// A message representing a book.</span>
<span class="kd">message</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nc">Book</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// Other fields...</span>

<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// The IETF BCP-47 language code representing the language in which</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// the book was originally written.</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="c1">// https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag</span>
<span class="w">  </span><span class="kt">string</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="na">language_code</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="o">=</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">99</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre></div>
<ul>
<li>Fields representing standardized concepts <strong>must</strong> use the appropriate data
  type for the standard code (usually <code>string</code>).<ul>
<li>Fields representing standardized concepts <strong>should not</strong> use enums, even if
  they only allow a small subset of possible values. Using enums in this
  situation often leads to frustrating lookup tables when using multiple APIs
  together.</li>
<li>Fields representing standardized concepts <strong>must</strong> indicate which standard
  they follow, preferably with a link (either to the standard itself, the
  Wikipedia description, or something similar).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The field name <strong>should</strong> end in <code>_code</code> or <code>_type</code> unless the concept has an
  obviously clearer suffix.</li>
<li>When accepting values provided by users, validation <strong>should</strong> be
  case-insensitive unless this would introduce ambiguity (for example, accept
  both <code>en-gb</code> and <code>en-GB</code>). When providing values to users, APIs <strong>should</strong>
  use the canonical case (in the example above, <code>en-GB</code>).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="content-types">Content types</h3>
<p>Fields representing a content or media type <strong>must</strong> use <a href="https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml">IANA media types</a>.
For legacy reasons, the field <strong>should</strong> be called <code>mime_type</code>.</p>
<h3 id="countries-and-regions">Countries and regions</h3>
<p>Fields representing individual countries or nations <strong>must</strong> use the <a href="http://cldr.unicode.org/">Unicode
CLDR region codes</a> (<a href="https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/46/supplemental/territory_information.html">list</a>), such as <code>US</code> or <code>CH</code>, and the field
<strong>must</strong> be called <code>region_code</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Important:</strong> Please read the <a href="#countryregion-field-naming">rationale</a> for this
requirement.</p>
<h3 id="currency">Currency</h3>
<p>Fields representing currency <strong>must</strong> use <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_4217">ISO-4217 currency codes</a>,
such as <code>USD</code> or <code>CHF</code>, and the field <strong>must</strong> be called <code>currency_code</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> For representing an amount of money in a particular currency, rather
than the currency code itself, use <a href="https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto"><code>google.type.Money</code></a>.</p>
<h3 id="language">Language</h3>
<p>Fields representing spoken languages <strong>must</strong> use <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag">IETF BCP-47 language
codes</a> (<a href="https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/46/supplemental/territory_information.html">list</a>), such as <code>en-US</code> or <code>de-CH</code>, and the field <strong>must</strong>
be called <code>language_code</code>.</p>
<h3 id="time-zones">Time zones</h3>
<p>Fields representing a time zone <strong>should</strong> use the <a href="http://www.iana.org/time-zones">IANA TZ</a> codes, and the
field <strong>must</strong> be called <code>time_zone</code>.</p>
<p>Fields also <strong>may</strong> represent a UTC offset rather than a time zone (note that
these are subtly different). In this case, the field <strong>must</strong> use the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Time_offsets_from_UTC">ISO-8601
format</a> to represent this, and the field <strong>must</strong> be named <code>utc_offset</code>.</p>
<h2 id="rationale">Rationale</h2>
<h3 id="countryregion-field-naming">Country/region field naming</h3>
<p>The use of <code>region_code</code> instead of <code>country_code</code> is critical to being able to
convey regions that are distinct from any country and to avoid any political
disputes associated with said region regarding their sovereignty or affiliation.
Google and many other companies are supporters of Unicode CLDR and standardize
their product internationalization efforts on Unicode CLDR, and APIs are no
different here. Furthermore, many of the values supported by Unicode CLDR are
not countries on their own, so using a more generic name is actually more
compatible with the specification.</p>
<h2 id="changelog">Changelog</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>2024-12-03</strong>: Strengthen rationale of country/region field naming</li>
<li><strong>2024-11-12</strong>: Change country/region code list to CLDR list from IANA list</li>
<li><strong>2020-05-12</strong>: Replaced <code>country_code</code> guidance with <code>region_code</code>,
  correcting an original error.</li>
</ul>
